citation_bill: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 22757–22757.6 (SB 942, Stats. 2024, ch. 291, as amended by AB 853, Stats. 2025, ch. 674)
short_title: California AI Transparency Act
status: in force (core chapter); delayed (platform/hosting 2027; capture devices 2028)
who_regulated: Covered GenAI providers (>1M monthly users, publicly accessible in CA); large online platforms (>2M unique monthly users); GenAI hosting platforms; capture-device manufacturers; third-party licensees of covered GenAI
hook: GenAI detection tool; optional manifest disclosure; required latent/provenance disclosure; platforms must detect/preserve provenance; hosting platforms may not knowingly host non-disclosing GenAI
carve_outs: Does not apply to products/services/sites/apps that provide exclusively non-user-generated video game, TV, streaming, movie, or interactive experiences (§ 22757.5). Large online platform excludes broadband and telecommunications services.
enforcer: Attorney General, city attorney, or county counsel
private_suit: none
statutory_damages: $5,000 civil penalty per violation (public enforcer); each day a discrete violation; attorney's fees to prevailing plaintiff in that public action. Not a private statutory-damages PRA.
plaintiffs_together: stacking — each day a discrete violation (§ 22757.4(b)); public action only
fee_shifting: yes — prevailing plaintiff (AG/city attorney/county counsel) reasonable attorney’s costs and fees (§ 22757.4(a)(2)); also fees on licensee injunction (§ 22757.4(c))
nexus: covered provider: GenAI system with >1,000,000 monthly visitors or users and publicly accessible within the geographic boundaries of the state (§ 22757.1(d)); hosting platform: download of source code/model weights by a resident of the state (§ 22757.1(g)); capture devices produced for sale in the state
out_of_state_actor: hosting platform that makes GenAI weights/code available for download by a resident of the state, regardless of compensation (§ 22757.1(g))
thresholds: >1,000,000 monthly visitors or users (covered provider); large online platform >2,000,000 unique monthly users in preceding 12 months
retroactivity: operative 2026-08-02 generally; platform/hosting 2027-01-01; capture devices first produced for sale in CA on/after 2028-01-01 — not a general retroactivity clause
ai_definition: GenAI system: an artificial intelligence that can generate derived synthetic content, including text, images, video, and audio, that emulates the structure and characteristics of the system’s training data (§ 22757.1)
record_retention: detection-tool content: not longer than necessary to comply; may not retain personal provenance data from submitted content (§ 22757.2(c)) — no year count
summary: Chapter 25 requires covered GenAI providers to offer a free detection tool, optional manifest labels, and latent provenance in image/video/audio outputs, and to contractually preserve that capability in licensees. AB 853 added large-platform provenance UI duties (operative 2027), hosting-platform bans on non-disclosing models (2027), and default latent capture-device watermarks for devices first produced for sale in CA on or after 1 Jan 2028. Enforcement is a $5,000-per-day civil penalty action by the AG, city attorney, or county counsel; the chapter does not create a consumer PRA.

short_title: Generative AI training data transparency
who_regulated: Developers that design, code, produce, or substantially modify a GenAI system/service for use by members of the public (systems released on/after 2022-01-01)
hook: Website documentation of training datasets (sources, types, IP status, PI, cleaning, collection window, synthetic data)
carve_outs: Affiliate/hospital medical-staff internal users excluded from 'members of the public.' No documentation required if the system's sole purpose is security and integrity; operation of aircraft in national airspace; or national security/military/defense made available only to a federal entity.
enforcer: unconfirmed — chaptered bill text reviewed through § 3111 contains no AG/CPPA/PRA clause
private_suit: unconfirmed (none in chaptered text reviewed)
statutory_damages: none in chaptered text reviewed
nexus: system or service made publicly available to Californians for use, regardless of compensation (§ 3111)
out_of_state_actor: silent (duty attaches when the system is made publicly available to Californians; no separate OOS-developer clause)
retroactivity: applies to GenAI released on or after 2022-01-01; first posting deadline 2026-01-01 (§ 3111)
federal_preemption: silent (national-security exception if made available only to a federal entity — not a preemption clause)
ai_definition: AI: engineered or machine-based system that varies in autonomy and can, for explicit or implicit objectives, infer from input how to generate outputs that can influence physical or virtual environments. GenAI: AI that can generate derived synthetic content such as text, images, video, and audio that emulates the structure and characteristics of the AI’s training data (§ 3110)
summary: By 1 Jan 2026 and before each public California release or substantial modification of a GenAI system first released on or after 1 Jan 2022, the developer must post high-level training-data documentation covering dataset sources, types, IP/license status, personal information, processing, collection dates, and synthetic-data use. The posting duty is public and website-based. The chaptered bill as reviewed does not itself state a private right of action, statutory damages, or a named enforcer; those items are unconfirmed from the statute.

citation_bill: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 22601–22606 (SB 243, Stats. 2025, ch. 677)
short_title: Companion chatbots
who_regulated: Operators that make a companion-chatbot platform available to a user in California
hook: Companion chatbot (anthropomorphic, relationship-sustaining GenAI); disclosure if a reasonable person would think it is human; self-harm protocol; extra minor safeguards
carve_outs: Not a companion chatbot: customer-service/ops/productivity bots; video-game bots limited to game topics; stand-alone speaker/voice-assistant devices that do not sustain a relationship or elicit emotional responses.
enforcer: Private suit under § 22604–22605; other law remains cumulative. No exclusive public enforcer named in the chapter.
private_suit: PRA
statutory_damages: $1,000 per violation or actual damages, whichever greater; plus injunctive relief and reasonable attorney's fees (§ 22605)
plaintiffs_together: stacking — $1,000 per violation or actual, whichever greater (§ 22605); plaintiff is a person who suffers injury in fact
fee_shifting: yes — injured person may recover reasonable attorney’s fees and costs (§ 22605(c))
nexus: operator: a person who makes a companion chatbot platform available to a user in the state (§ 22601(e))
out_of_state_actor: silent (hook is making the platform available to a user in the state)
federal_preemption: silent (sexually explicit conduct cross-cites 18 U.S.C. § 2256 — definitional, not preemption)
ai_definition: AI: engineered or machine-based system that varies in autonomy and can, for explicit or implicit objectives, infer from the input it receives how to generate outputs that can influence physical or virtual environments (§ 22601(a))
summary: Operators of companion-chatbot platforms must disclose that the bot is not human when a reasonable person would be misled, maintain and publish a protocol to prevent suicidal/self-harm content (including crisis-line referrals), and, for known minors, disclose AI use, remind every three hours, and block specified sexual content. Beginning 1 Jul 2027 operators must annually report crisis referrals and protocols to the Office of Suicide Prevention. A person who suffers injury in fact may sue for the greater of actual damages or $1,000 per violation, injunction, and fees.

short_title: Health care professions: deceptive AI terms or letters
who_regulated: Persons/entities that develop or deploy AI or GenAI whose advertising or functionality uses healing-arts titles, letters, or phrases
hook: AI/GenAI that implies licensed human health-care professional advice, care, reports, or assessments
carve_outs: Does not create a standalone insurance-code duty. Limited to terms regulated in BPC Division 2 (healing arts).
enforcer: Appropriate health-care professional licensing board or enforcement agency; injunctive relief under BPC § 125.5. Also expands existing criminal title-use prohibitions.
private_suit: none in this chapter
statutory_damages: none specified in this chapter (each use is a separate violation; penalties track underlying healing-arts title statutes — amounts unconfirmed here)
fee_shifting: silent in this chapter (injunction under BPC § 125.5)
nexus: silent in this chapter (developers/deployers of AI/GenAI using healing-arts titles; no in-state hook restated here)
criminal_overlay: also crime — act expands existing title-use crimes (reimbursement finding: creates a new crime/infraction or changes the definition of a crime)
ai_definition: AI has the meaning in Gov. Code § 11546.45.5; GenAI has the meaning in Gov. Code § 11549.64 (§ 4999.8)
summary: AB 489 makes existing healing-arts title-protection statutes enforceable against developers and deployers of AI/GenAI that use licensed titles in advertising or functionality, and independently prohibits AI from implying that care/advice is provided by a licensed natural person. Each use of a prohibited term is a separate violation. Boards may seek injunctions; the bill expands the scope of existing crimes rather than creating a consumer PRA.

citation_bill: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 1367.01(k); Cal. Ins. Code § 10123.135(j) (SB 1120, Stats. 2024, ch. 879)
short_title: Health coverage utilization review: AI, algorithms, and software tools
who_regulated: Knox-Keene health care service plans (DMHC), including specialized plans, and disability insurers covering hospital/medical/surgical (CDI), plus UR/UM contractors and delegated medical groups/IPAs
hook: AI, algorithm, or other software tool used for utilization review/management based in whole or in part on medical necessity
carve_outs: Medi-Cal managed care only to the extent DHCS obtains federal approvals and FFP is not jeopardized. Prayer/spiritual healing exception in HSC § 1367.01(m) remains. Does not recast a plan/insurer as a 'health care provider' for MICRA-type statutes.
enforcer: DMHC Director (administrative penalties; medical survey) for plans; Insurance Commissioner (administrative penalties) for disability insurers. Willful Knox-Keene violation remains a crime.
private_suit: none created by SB 1120 (existing Knox-Keene/Insurance Code remedies unconfirmed as a new PRA)
statutory_damages: none specified in the AI subdivisions; administrative penalties under existing UR statutes (amounts not restated in the AI add-on)
cure_period: none specific to the AI subdivisions
nexus: silent in the AI add-on (Knox-Keene plans and specified disability insurers; no issued/delivered clause in SB 1120 text reviewed)
insurance_situs: silent (no delivered/issued-in-state clause in the AI subdivisions; UR/UM of covered plans/insurers)
criminal_overlay: also crime — willful Knox-Keene violation remains a crime (existing overlay; SB 1120 does not restate it in the AI subdivisions)
federal_preemption: silent (Medi-Cal only to the extent DHCS obtains federal approvals — not a preemption clause)
ai_definition: silent as a standalone AI definition; statute regulates an AI, algorithm, or other software tool used for UR/UM based in whole or in part on medical necessity
summary: Plans and disability insurers that use AI/algorithms/software for medical-necessity UR/UM, or that contract with entities that do, must base tool determinations on the individual clinical record (not solely a group dataset), apply criteria fairly and without unlawful discrimination, keep the tool auditable, disclose use in UR policies, and periodically review performance. The tool may not deny, delay, or modify services on medical necessity; only a licensed physician or competent licensed clinician may make that determination after reviewing the request and clinical history.

citation_bill: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 1339.75 (AB 3030, Stats. 2024, ch. 848)
short_title: Artificial intelligence in health care services (patient communications)
who_regulated: Health facilities, clinics, physician offices, and group-practice offices that use GenAI to generate written or verbal patient communications about clinical information
hook: GenAI-generated patient clinical communications (not mere billing/scheduling)
carve_outs: If a human licensed/certified provider reads and reviews the communication, the disclaimer/contact duties do not apply. Administrative/billing/scheduling communications are outside 'patient clinical information.'
enforcer: CDPH facility/clinic licensing enforcement (HSC arts. starting §§ 1275 and 1225); Medical Board or Osteopathic Medical Board for physicians
private_suit: none in this section
statutory_damages: none in this section
nexus: silent in § 1339.75 (health facilities, clinics, physician/group offices; no extra in-state hook)
safe_harbor: duties do not apply if a licensed/certified human provider reads and reviews the communication (§ 1339.75)
criminal_overlay: civil-only (existing facility/board enforcement; no new crime in this section)
ai_definition: silent in this section beyond generative artificial intelligence used to generate patient clinical communications
summary: Covered providers that use GenAI to generate clinical patient communications must include a medium-specific disclaimer that the communication was AI-generated and clear instructions to reach a human. The duty does not apply if a licensed/certified human provider reads and reviews the output. Violations run through existing facility, clinic, and medical-board enforcement, not a new PRA.

short_title: Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act
operative_date: same as effective (CalCompute consortium operative only upon appropriation)
who_regulated: Frontier developers (foundation models trained above 10^26 FLOP); additional duties on large frontier developers (>$500M prior-year group revenue)
hook: Frontier/foundation models and catastrophic-risk governance, transparency reports, critical-safety-incident reporting, whistleblower protections
carve_outs: Does not apply to the extent of a strict conflict with a federal-government contract or federal preemption. Preempts local catastrophic-risk rules adopted on/after 2025-01-01. Equity-value loss is not 'property' damage. Redactions allowed for trade secrets, cybersecurity, public safety, national security.
enforcer: Attorney General (civil penalty for TFAIA noncompliance). OES receives incident/risk reports. Whistleblower civil action under Labor Code § 1107.1.
private_suit: none for the BPC transparency chapter; PAG/PRA for covered-employee whistleblower claims (Lab. Code § 1107.1, fees to successful plaintiff)
statutory_damages: AG civil penalty not to exceed $1,000,000 per violation (severity-dependent) for specified TFAIA breaches. Whistleblower chapter: no liquidated amount; fees authorized.
fee_shifting: yes — court may award reasonable attorney’s fees to a plaintiff who brings a successful whistleblower action (Lab. Code § 1107.1(f)); BPC AG penalties silent on private fees
nexus: silent (frontier/large-frontier developer definitions are compute/revenue, not residence)
thresholds: frontier model: trained using computing power greater than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations; large frontier developer: >$500,000,000 prior-year group revenue (chaptered SB 53)
local_preemption: yes — preempts any local rule/ordinance adopted on or after 2025-01-01 specifically related to regulation of frontier developers’ management of catastrophic risk (SB 53)
criminal_overlay: civil-only (BPC civil penalty + labor whistleblower civil action)
federal_preemption: cite — act shall not apply to the extent it strictly conflicts with a federal-government-entity contract, and shall not apply to the extent it is preempted by federal law (SB 53)
ai_definition: frontier/foundation model: foundation model trained above 10^26 FLOP; foundation model = AI model trained on a broad data set, designed for generality of output, adaptable to a wide range of distinctive tasks (SB 53)
impact_assessment_discoverable: silent (framework/transparency reports are public-facing with redactions; no private-discovery clause)
record_retention: silent as a year count (incident reporting windows 15 days / 24 hours)
summary: Large frontier developers must publish and follow a frontier AI framework covering catastrophic-risk thresholds, mitigations, third-party evaluation, cybersecurity of unreleased weights, and incident response, plus quarterly internal-use risk summaries to OES. All frontier developers must publish a transparency report on deploy and report critical safety incidents (15 days, or 24 hours if imminent death/serious injury). The AG may recover up to $1 million per violation of specified duties. Covered employees have anti-retaliation and anonymous internal-reporting rights; successful whistleblower plaintiffs may recover attorney's fees.

citation_bill: Cal. Lab. Code § 927 (AB 2602, Stats. 2024) — digital replica contract clause
short_title: Digital replica clauses in personal/professional services contracts
enacted_date: 2024 (chaptered; confirm exact day on LegInfo bill history)
operative_date: Applies to new performances fixed on or after 2025-01-01
who_regulated: Parties to personal/professional services agreements that purport to authorize a digital replica of an individual's voice or likeness
hook: Computer-generated highly realistic digital replica of voice/visual likeness used in lieu of the individual's performance
carve_outs: Clause remains enforceable if specified conditions (including reasonably specific intended uses, and union representation where applicable) are met — exact remaining conditions should be read from § 927. First Amendment/work-consistent uses described in the statute.
enforcer: Contract unenforceability (private litigation); no new public enforcer in the bill digest reviewed
private_suit: PRA (as contract unenforceability / existing civil remedies); not a new statutory-damages PRA
statutory_damages: none in the bill text reviewed (unenforceability, not liquidated damages)
nexus: silent
retroactivity: unenforceability only as to a new performance fixed on or after 2025-01-01 (§ 927(a))
safe_harbor: clause remains enforceable if reasonably specific intended uses (or uses consistent with the contract and fundamental character) and specified counsel/union representation (§ 927(a)(2)–(3))
ai_definition: n/a as AI/ADS — digital replica means a computer-generated, highly realistic electronic representation readily identifiable as the voice or visual likeness of an individual (§ 927(c))
summary: A contract clause that allows a new digital-replica performance of an individual, fixed on or after 1 Jan 2025, is unenforceable as to that replica if statutory conditions on consent and description of intended uses are not met. 'Digital replica' is a computer-generated highly realistic electronic representation readily identifiable as the person's voice or visual likeness. The remedy in the chaptered bill is unenforceability of the replica clause, not a new liquidated-damages PRA.

short_title: Deceased personality digital replica
operative_date: same as effective (post-mortem right remains 70 years)
who_regulated: Persons who produce, distribute, or make available the digital replica of a deceased personality's voice or likeness in an expressive audiovisual work or sound recording without prior consent from the post-mortem rights holder (and, for professional musicians, exclusive recording/distribution counterparties per (n))
hook: Deceased-personality digital replica in expressive AV works / sound recordings (computer-generated highly realistic voice or likeness)
carve_outs: News, public affairs, or sports; comment, criticism, scholarship, satire, or parody; documentary/historical/biographical representation (including some fictionalization) unless intended to and does create a false impression that the work is an authentic recording; fleeting/incidental use; ads for those exempt works. Advertising-media owners/employees lack liability without knowledge (§ 3344.1(l)). No express insurance/GLBA carve-out in text reviewed.
enforcer: Private rights-holders (PRA)
private_suit: PRA
statutory_damages: Greater of $10,000 or actual damages suffered by a person controlling the rights to the deceased personality's likeness (§ 3344.1(a)(2)(A)(i)). Preexisting merchandise/ad cause of action remains greater of $750 or actual, plus profits/punitive/fees. No cure.
plaintiffs_together: prevailing party or parties; rights-holder controlling the deceased personality’s likeness (§ 3344.1)
fee_shifting: yes — prevailing party or parties entitled to attorney’s fees and costs (§ 3344.1)
nexus: quote — liability and damages arise from acts occurring directly in this state; acts giving rise to liability limited to use on or in products, merchandise, goods, or services, or the advertising or selling or soliciting of purchases of products etc. (§ 3344.1)
no_extraterritorial_clause: yes — liability/damages limited to acts occurring directly in this state (§ 3344.1)
retroactivity: quote — rights recognized by this section are expressly made retroactive, including to deceased personalities who died prior to January 1, 1985 (§ 3344.1(q))
ai_definition: n/a as AI/ADS — digital replica of deceased personality’s voice or likeness (computer-generated highly realistic)
summary: AB 1836 adds Civ. Code § 3344.1(a)(2): producing, distributing, or making available a digital replica of a deceased personality's voice or likeness in an expressive audiovisual work or sound recording without specified prior consent is independently actionable. The plaintiff may recover the greater of $10,000 or actual damages. First Amendment-style exemptions are in (a)(2)(A)(ii). This is not a general deepfake-porn statute.

citation_bill: C.R.S. §§ 6-1-1701 et seq. as reenacted by SB 26-189 (2026 Sess. Laws ch. 131); repeals/replaces SB 24-205
short_title: Automated Decision-Making Technology in Consequential Decisions
operative_date: 2027-01-01; applies to decisions on or after that date (developer documentation duties also start then)
who_regulated: Developers and deployers of covered ADMT that materially influences a consequential decision (education, employment, housing, financial/lending, insurance, health care, essential government services/public benefits)
hook: Automated decision-making technology (predictions/recommendations/classifications/rankings/scores) that materially influences a consequential decision, including insurance
carve_outs: Session-law 6-1-1708(1)(a) (2026 Ch. 131): an insurer as defined in § 10-1-102(13) and affiliated entities subject to § 10-3-1104.9 ARE IN COMPLIANCE WITH THIS PART 17 IN THE PRACTICE OF INSURANCE. (1)(b) fallback: if not deemed in compliance, insurer still must give 6-1-1704(3) adverse-outcome notice to the extent applicable. (2) employment / employment-opportunity ADMT is NOT carved out. (6) GLBA is a disclosure limit (no duty to disclose nonpublic personal information in a manner that would violate GLBA), not an entity exemption. HIPAA covered entities/BAs: 6-1-1701–1706 do not apply except employment ADMT (health-care providers only if operating from a Colorado location). No <50-FTE deployer exemption (that SB 24-205 relief did not survive). No new PRA (6-1-1709).
enforcer: Colorado Attorney General exclusive for the ADMT disclosure/consumer-rights duties (6-1-1706); violation = CCPA deceptive trade practice
private_suit: none (6-1-1709: nothing in part 17 creates a new private right of action; AG exclusive for 6-1-1702–1705 via CCPA DTP)
statutory_damages: none private. Violation is a deceptive trade practice (6-1-105(1)(uuuu); 6-1-1706). CCPA AG civil penalties (commonly 6-1-112) — amounts not restated in Ch. 131.
cure_period: 60-day notice-and-cure if cure is possible, for AG actions initiated before 2030-01-01 (legislative summary)
class_collective: silent (no class bar/invitation; 6-1-1706(6) preserves CRCP 19/20 joinder for existing-law actions)
plaintiffs_together: no new PRA (6-1-1709 / 6-1-1706(4)); CRCP 19 and 20 joinder allowed in actions arising under existing law (6-1-1706(6)); fault allocated by relative fault; no new joint-and-several (6-1-1707)
fee_shifting: silent in part 17 (CCPA AG enforcement vehicle)
notice_cure: 60-day AG notice-and-cure if AG deems cure possible, before enforcement; not required if knowing or repeated violation; subsection (3) repeal 2030-01-01 (6-1-1706(3))
nexus: deployer = person doing business in Colorado that deploys a covered ADMT; developer = person doing business in Colorado that develops/offers/sells/leases/licenses covered ADMT; consumer includes employee, CO-resident job applicant, and any individual whose access/eligibility/opportunity in Colorado is evaluated in a consequential decision by a person doing business in Colorado (6-1-1701)
out_of_state_actor: silent as a labeled OOS-developer clause (hook is doing business in Colorado)
insurance_situs: silent (insurance is a covered domain including underwriting, pricing, coverage, claims adjudication; 6-1-1708 deemed-compliance for 10-3-1104.9 insurers in the practice of insurance — no issued/delivered clause)
retroactivity: applies to decisions on or after 2027-01-01 (session law)
federal_preemption: silent (GLBA cited as a disclosure limit, 6-1-1708(6); FERPA/HIPAA exemptions — not a preemption clause)
ai_definition: covered ADMT: automated decision-making technology used to materially influence a consequential decision (predictions/recommendations/classifications/rankings/scores) (6-1-1701)
impact_assessment_discoverable: silent (developer/deployer must retain compliance records >=3 years; no private-discovery clause; no PRA)
waiver_indemnity_ban: yes — developer-deployer indemnity for own acts/omissions related to ADMT use in CADA/other CO anti-discrimination violations is contrary to public policy and void (6-1-1707(7))
record_retention: developer: not less than 3 years after creation of a record required under 6-1-1702; deployer: not less than 3 years after the date of a consequential decision (6-1-1702(4), 6-1-1703)
summary: SB 26-189 repeals the never-operative 2024 high-risk AI act and, effective 1 Jan 2027, regulates ADMT used to materially influence consequential decisions, expressly including insurance. Insurers subject to § 10-3-1104.9 are in compliance with part 17 in the practice of insurance (6-1-1708(1)(a)); employment ADMT remains covered; GLBA limits disclosures rather than exempting the entity. 6-1-1709: no new PRA. AG enforces as a deceptive trade practice, with a 60-day cure before 2030 if cure is possible.

citation_bill: C.R.S. §§ 6-1-1701 et seq. as originally added by SB 24-205 (2024); delayed by SB 25B-004; repealed/replaced by SB 26-189
short_title: Consumer Protections for Artificial Intelligence (original Colorado AI Act)
effective_date: Originally 2026-02-01; postponed to 2026-06-30 by 2025 extraordinary-session bill
operative_date: Never operative. Replaced 2026-05-14, before the postponed 2026-06-30 date.
who_regulated: Would have covered developers and deployers of high-risk AI systems used in consequential decisions
hook: High-risk AI / algorithmic discrimination (historical only)
carve_outs: n/a — not in force
enforcer: n/a
private_suit: none (was AG-only in the 2024 act)
statutory_damages: none
plaintiffs_together: no PRA (original 6-1-1706(6): part 17 not a basis for and not subject to a private right of action)
notice_cure: affirmative defense if discover-and-cure via feedback/red-team/internal review and NIST/ISO 42001 (or designated) RMF (original 6-1-1706(3)) — not a pre-suit notice period
nexus: consumer = Colorado resident; deployer/developer = person doing business in this state (original 6-1-1701)
insurance_situs: n/a (never operative; original 6-1-1705(7) deemed insurers in full compliance if subject to 10-3-1104.9)
thresholds: <50 FTE deployer exemption from specified IA/risk-policy duties if other conditions met (original 6-1-1703(6))
retroactivity: never operative; duties were slated on/after 2026-02-01 then postponed; repealed/replaced 2026-05-14
safe_harbor: NIST AI RMF / ISO 42001 (or designated equivalent) as affirmative defense to AG action (original 6-1-1706(3))
local_preemption: silent (original 6-1-1706(5): AG exclusive enforcement does not preempt other rights/claims)
federal_preemption: silent (federal-agency-approved systems and HIPAA covered-entity health recommendations carved out)
ai_definition: AI system: any machine-based system that, for any explicit or implicit objective, infers from the inputs the system receives how to generate outputs, including content, decisions, predictions, or recommendations, that can influence physical or virtual environments (original 6-1-1701(2))
impact_assessment_discoverable: no as to CORA — IA/risk policy disclosed to AG are not subject to Colorado Open Records Act; AG disclosure does not waive attorney-client/work product (original 6-1-1703(9)). Statute silent on private-suit discovery (and there was no PRA).
record_retention: IA and related records at least 3 years following final deployment (original 6-1-1703(3)(f))
summary: Colorado's 2024 high-risk AI consumer statute was signed 17 May 2024 with a 1 Feb 2026 effective date, later pushed to 30 Jun 2026. A federal challenge and stay in spring 2026 preceded SB 26-189, which repealed and reenacted part 17 before either date arrived. Do not treat SB 24-205 as a current holding; the operative regime, when it starts, is SB 26-189.

short_title: Insurers' use of ECDIS, algorithms, and predictive models — unfair discrimination prohibited
operative_date: Direct unfair-discrimination ban in force; testing/governance duties operate through Division of Insurance rules by line (life, PPA auto, health benefit plans among those with adopted rules)
who_regulated: Insurers as to insurance practices (marketing, underwriting, pricing, utilization management, reimbursement, claims)
hook: External consumer data and information sources and algorithms/predictive models using ECDIS that unfairly discriminate on listed protected classes
carve_outs: Title insurance; surety bonds under part 3 of art. 4 of title 10; commercial policies except BOP/CGL with annual premium of $10,000 or less. Does not require collection of race etc. Does not, standing alone, prohibit specified traditional medical/family/occupational underwriting for life/annuity/LTC/disability unless those factors sit inside a tested ECDIS model.
enforcer: Commissioner of Insurance (examine/investigate under § 10-3-1106; part 11 unfair-practices orders/penalties)
private_suit: none created by § 10-3-1104.9 (confidentiality of filings vs private discovery is express)
statutory_damages: none in this section
cure_period: Rules must include a reasonable period for insurers to remedy unfairly discriminatory impact (§ 10-3-1104.9(3)(c)(I))
notice_cure: rules must include a reasonable period for insurers to remedy unfairly discriminatory impact (§ 10-3-1104.9(3)(c)(I))
nexus: silent as a residence clause (insurer insurance practices); legislative declaration refers to Colorado residents’ access to insurance products
insurance_situs: claims — insurance practice means marketing, underwriting, pricing, utilization management, reimbursement methodologies, and claims management in the transaction of insurance (§ 10-3-1104.9(8)(c)); issued/delivered-in-state silent
thresholds: none (line carve-outs are title, surety, most commercial; small BOP/CGL with annual premium <=$10,000 remain in)
safe_harbor: rules must allow use of ECDIS/models previously assessed by the Division and found not unfairly discriminatory (§ 10-3-1104.9(3)(c)(II))
criminal_overlay: civil-only in this section (DOI examine/unfair-practices tools)
ai_definition: algorithm: computational or machine learning process that informs human decision making in insurance practices; predictive model: mathematical/computational methods examining datasets for patterns and calculating probability of an outcome (§ 10-3-1104.9(8))
impact_assessment_discoverable: no — filings obtained/created/disclosed pursuant to this section are confidential/privileged, not CORA, not subject to subpoena, and not subject to discovery or admissible in any private civil action (§ 10-3-1104.9(3)(d))
record_retention: silent as a year count (risk-management framework on a continuous basis)
summary: In addition to existing unfair-discrimination bans, an insurer may not, pursuant to commissioner rules, use ECDIS or algorithms/predictive models using ECDIS in a way that unfairly discriminates on race, color, national/ethnic origin, religion, sex, sexual orientation, disability, gender identity, or gender expression. citation_bill: 740 ILCS 14/1–25 (BIPA; SB 2979 / P.A. 103-0769 (2024) amending damages)

who_regulated: Private entities that possess, collect, capture, purchase, receive through trade, or otherwise obtain biometric identifiers/information of Illinois persons (and that disclose/sell them)
hook: Biometric identifiers (retina/iris scan, fingerprint, voiceprint, scan of hand or face geometry) and biometric information — highly relevant to AI face/voice systems. Excludes writing samples, photos as such, donated organs, etc. per § 10.

enforcer: Private plaintiffs (circuit court or supplemental federal claim). No exclusive AG PRA substitute.
private_suit: PRA
statutory_damages: $1,000 liquidated or actual, whichever greater, per negligent violation; $5,000 liquidated or actual, whichever greater, per intentional/reckless violation; plus fees/costs and injunction. Cap: at most one recovery per person for repeated same-method collection or same-recipient disclosure of the same biometric (14/20(b)–(c)).
class_collective: silent (no class bar or invitation in the Act)
plaintiffs_together: one-recovery — repeated same-method collection of the same biometric of the same person is a single §15(b) violation with at most one recovery; same-recipient disclosure of the same biometric is a single §15(d) violation with at most one recovery (740 ILCS 14/20(b)–(c))
fee_shifting: yes — prevailing party may recover reasonable attorneys' fees and costs (14/20)
nexus: silent as a statutory residence/transaction clause (legislative findings mention locations in this State; private entity is not geographically limited in §10)
retroactivity: 2024 damages amendment (P.A. 103-0769) effective 2024-08-02; silent as to pre-2008 conduct
federal_preemption: cite — shall not be deemed to apply to a financial institution or affiliate subject to GLBA Title V (14/25(c)); shall not be construed to conflict with HIPAA or the X-Ray Retention Act (14/25(b))
ai_definition: n/a as AI/ADS — biometric identifier (retina/iris scan, fingerprint, voiceprint, scan of hand or face geometry) and biometric information (14/10)
impact_assessment_discoverable: silent (14/25(a): nothing impacts admission or discovery of biometrics in any action)
record_retention: public written retention schedule and destruction when purpose satisfied or within 3 years of last interaction, whichever earlier (14/15(a))
summary: BIPA requires a public retention/destruction schedule, written notice and a release before collection, a prohibition on sale, and disclosure limits for biometric identifiers and information. Aggrieved persons may sue for the greater of actual or liquidated damages ($1,000 negligent / $5,000 intentional or reckless), fees, and an injunction. The 2024 amendment, effective 2 Aug 2024, treats repeated same-method collections or same-recipient disclosures of the same person's biometric as a single recoverable violation. GLBA-covered financial institutions are carved out.

citation_bill: 765 ILCS 1075/ (Right of Publicity Act as amended by HB 4875, P.A. 103-0836)

enforcer: Private — individual, transferee, post-mortem holders; recording artists and exclusive audio licensees (1075/20(a-5))
private_suit: PRA

fee_shifting: yes — court may award prevailing party reasonable attorney's fees, costs, and expenses (1075/55)
nexus: silent in §§30/40 as compiled (commercial use of identity; knowing distribution of a work containing an unauthorized digital replica)

limitations_period: silent in the compiled sections reviewed

summary: P.A. 103-0836 adds digital-replica liability to Illinois's Right of Publicity Act. Knowingly distributing a sound recording or audiovisual work that contains an unauthorized digital replica is actionable. The identity holder (and specified recording-industry counterparties) may recover the greater of actual damages plus profits or $1,000, and punitive damages if the violation is willful. News/satire/documentary and § 230/512-style safe harbors apply. There is no insurance or GLBA carve-out.

citation_bill: 740 ILCS 190/ (Civil Remedies for Nonconsensual Dissemination of Private Sexual Images Act; digitally-altered hook P.A. 103-0294, further am. P.A. 103-571)

enforcer: Depicted individual (PRA). SOL generally 2 years from discovery of dissemination or from threat (190/30).
private_suit: PRA
statutory_damages: Greater of actual economic/noneconomic (incl. emotional distress) or statutory damages not to exceed $10,000 against each defendant for all disseminations/threats known at filing or during the action; plus defendant's monetary gain; punitive; fees/costs; injunction (190/25). plaintiffs_together: one-recovery/stacking — statutory damages not to exceed $10,000 against each defendant for all disseminations/threats known at filing or during the action (190/25)

summary: Illinois's civil NCII statute reaches intentionally digitally altered sexual images. The depicted person may recover the greater of actual damages (including emotional distress) or statutory damages capped at $10,000 per defendant for all known disseminations, plus the defendant's monetary gain, punitive damages, fees, and an injunction. A disclaimer that the image was altered is not a defense. There is no insurance or GLBA carve-out.

citation_bill: Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act, SB 315 / P.A. 104-0538 (compiled ILCS chapter not in the ILCS tree as of 2026-09-02; use the Public Act). AI defined by cross-reference to 815 ILCS 550/5.

statutory_damages: AG civil penalty not exceeding $1,000,000 first violation / $3,000,000 each subsequent; plus $1,000 per day for §18 disclosure failures/false information. Not private damages.
cure_period: unconfirmed as a general pre-suit cure; §18 daily penalty follows notice and hearing
plaintiffs_together: none — §25(d) nothing in this Act shall be construed to establish a private right of action

thresholds: frontier model: foundation model trained using computing power greater than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations; large frontier developer: with affiliates, prior-year annual gross revenues in excess of $500,000,000
retroactivity: effective 2027-01-01; framework/audit 2028-01-01 or 90 days after first qualifying as a large frontier developer, whichever later

summary: AISMA, approved 6 Jul 2026 and effective 1 Jan 2027 (framework/audit 1 Jan 2028), is Illinois's frontier-model safety statute. ai_definition: silent (quote Elec. Law §§ 14-106 / 14-107-a on official compilation before advising)

citation_bill: N.Y. Gen. Bus. Law art. 44-B, §§ 1420 et seq. (RAISE Act, S.6953-B / A.6453-B, Ch. 699 of 2025, as amended Ch. 96 of 2026)
short_title: Responsible AI Safety and Education (RAISE) Act
effective_date: 2027-01-01 (as reported from chapter materials; confirm in Ch. 699/96 effective clause)
who_regulated: Developers of frontier AI models (compute/capability thresholds in the article)
hook: Frontier model training, safety frameworks, transparency, incident reporting
carve_outs: Preemption/local rules and smaller-model exclusions are in the article — confirm before scoping a client. Not an insurance-underwriting statute.
enforcer: Attorney General (civil penalties). Secondary sources cite up to $1,000,000 first / $3,000,000 subsequent — those figures are unconfirmed from official GBL text in this pass.
private_suit: unconfirmed (likely none; do not assert PRA)
statutory_damages: AG civil penalties — amounts unconfirmed from official compilation in this pass
fee_shifting: silent in S.6953-B text reviewed (AG civil penalties)
nexus: article shall only apply to frontier models that are developed, deployed, or operating in whole or in part in New York state (§ 1424 as in S.6953-B)
out_of_state_actor: silent (in-whole-or-in-part in NY is the hook, not a labeled OOS-developer clause)
thresholds: frontier model: AI model trained using greater than 10^26 computational operations (integer or floating-point) the compute cost of which exceeds $100,000,000, or a distillation of such a model with compute cost exceeding $5,000,000; large developer: trained at least one frontier model and spent over $100,000,000 in compute costs in aggregate (S.6953-B — confirm Ch. 96 amendments before relying on dollar figures)
criminal_overlay: civil-only (AG penalties in S.6953-B; PRA not found in that bill text)
federal_preemption: silent (redactions only to the extent required by federal law, in the AG/DHSES protocol-access clause)
ai_definition: AI: machine-based system that infers how to generate outputs from inputs using computational, statistical, or machine-learning techniques (S.6953-B definitions)
record_retention: unredacted safety-and-security protocol and specified test records retained for as long as a frontier model is deployed plus five years (S.6953-B)
summary: New York's RAISE Act, signed December 2025 and chapter-amended March 2026, will impose frontier-model safety frameworks, transparency, and incident-reporting duties, currently slated for 1 Jan 2027. It is a developer-safety statute, not a consumer ADMT or insurance-code law. Penalty amounts and PRA status should be taken from GBL §§ 1420–1429 once the official compilation is pulled; they are unconfirmed here.

citation_bill: N.Y. Gen. Bus. Law § 349-a (L. 2025 ch. 58 Part X; old 349-a renumbered 349-h)
short_title: Personalized algorithmic pricing
who_regulated: Any entity that sets the price of a specific good or service using personalized algorithmic pricing (dynamic pricing set by an algorithm that uses personal data) and advertises/offers that price to a consumer in New York using personal data specific to that consumer
hook: ADS / automated pricing (algorithm + personal data); not limited to 'AI' by name
carve_outs: (a) person/firm subject to the Insurance Law or regulations thereunder; (b) GLBA Title V financial institutions and affiliates (15 U.S.C. § 6809 / § 6801 et seq.) to the extent subject to GLBA; (c) financial institution as defined in Financial Services Law § 801(f); (d) subscription-contract price lower than the contracted price. For-hire/TNC location data used solely to compute mileage/time fares excluded from 'personal data.'
enforcer: NY AG. Must first send a cease-and-desist letter with a designated cure timeline; only after continued violation may AG seek injunction.
private_suit: none (AG-only; special proceeding for injunction). Does not limit other civil/criminal liability.
statutory_damages: After C&D + continued violation: injunction without proof of injury; civil penalty not more than $1,000 per violation. Public penalty, not a private liquidated-damages PRA.
cure_period: Designated timeline in the AG cease-and-desist letter
notice_cure: AG must first send a cease-and-desist letter specifying alleged violations and remedies to cure within a designated timeline; only after continued violation may AG seek injunction/penalty (GBL § 349-a)
nexus: entity domiciled or doing business in New York state; advertises personalized algorithmic pricing to a consumer in New York using personal data specific to that consumer (§ 349-a)
out_of_state_actor: silent (domiciled or doing business in NY + offer to a NY consumer)
insurance_situs: n/a (section does not apply to a person/firm subject to the Insurance Law or regulations thereunder; also GLBA Title V FIs/affiliates and FSL § 801(f) FIs)
criminal_overlay: civil-only as this section (does not limit other civil or criminal liability)
federal_preemption: silent (GLBA is an entity carve-out, not a preemption clause)
ai_definition: personalized algorithmic pricing: dynamic pricing set by an algorithm that uses personal data (not limited to AI by name) (§ 349-a)
summary: Effective 8 Jul 2025, an entity that advertises a price set by personalized algorithmic pricing to a New York consumer using that consumer's personal data must disclose that the price was set by an algorithm using personal data. The section does not apply to persons subject to the Insurance Law or insurance regulations, GLBA Title V FIs/affiliates, or FSL § 801(f) FIs. The AG enforces after a C&D letter; there is no consumer PRA. Civil penalty not more than $1,000 per violation after continued noncompliance.

short_title: AI companion models
who_regulated: Operators providing an AI companion to a user using it for personal use in New York. Conjunctive definition: retains session/preference info to personalize; asks unprompted emotion-based questions beyond a direct response; sustains ongoing dialogue on matters personal to the user.
hook: Companion chatbot disclosure + suicide/self-harm protocol
carve_outs: Not an AI companion: (i) customer-service / commercial-product-info only; (ii) primarily designed and marketed for efficiency, research, or technical assistance; (iii) internal business / employee productivity. No Insurance Law or GLBA carve-out.
enforcer: NY AG only (injunction + civil penalties). Penalties go to a suicide prevention fund (St. Fin. L. § 99-ss).
private_suit: none (AG-only; no PRA in Art. 47)
statutory_damages: Up to $15,000 per day for violations of §§ 1701 or 1702; other court-deemed remedies. Public penalty, not a private PRA.
fee_shifting: silent (AG injunction + civil penalties to suicide-prevention fund)
nexus: operator providing an AI companion to a user using it for personal use in New York (Art. 47)
ai_definition: AI companion (conjunctive): retains session/preference info to personalize; asks unprompted emotion-based questions beyond a direct response; sustains ongoing dialogue on matters personal to the user (L. 2025 ch. 58 Part U)
summary: In force 5 Nov 2025, GBL Art. 47 requires operators of AI companions used personally in New York to run a reasonable-efforts self-harm protocol with crisis referrals and to disclose that the user is not communicating with a human at the start of an interaction (need not exceed once per day) and at least every three hours if the session continues. The AG enforces; civil penalties up to $15,000 per day. No PRA and no Insurance Law/GLBA carve-out. Do not import secondary-source extras (16-pt type, Department of State reports) that are not in chaptered Part U.

citation_bill: N.Y. Civ. Rights Law §§ 52-c, 52-b; Penal L. § 245.15 as amd. L. 2023 ch. 513 and L. 2024 ch. 58 Part MM Subpart A
short_title: Intimate-image digitization (CRL 52-c / 52-b)
who_regulated: Actors who disseminate/publish or (52-c) threaten to disseminate intimate/sexually explicit stills or video, including images created or altered by digitization (another person's image or computer-generated images; 52-c names software/ML/AI)
hook: Deepfake / intimate image
carve_outs: Penal: reporting unlawful conduct; lawful LE/legal/medical; voluntary public/commercial exposure; legitimate public purpose; § 230. Civil statutes have consent and First Amendment-adjacent limits as written. No insurance/GLBA carve-out.
enforcer: DAs (criminal); private plaintiffs (civil)
private_suit: PRA (CRL § 52-c digitized sexually explicit depiction; CRL § 52-b intimate image including digitization). Penal is criminal only.
statutory_damages: CRL § 52-c: injunction, compensatory + punitive, costs/fees. No liquidated per-image schedule in the civil-rights sections as compiled. Penal § 245.15: class A misdemeanor.
fee_shifting: yes — costs/fees authorized in CRL 52-c/52-b civil actions (as compiled)
nexus: 52-b: still/video depicting an unclothed intimate part of a resident of this state, or a resident engaging in sexual conduct, hosted or transmitted without consent — defendant subject to personal jurisdiction in this state to the maximum extent permitted under the U.S. Constitution and federal law (Ch. 58 2024 Part MM). 52-c: dissemination/threat of digitized sexually explicit depiction.
out_of_state_actor: express PJ hook for host/transmitter of a NY resident's intimate image to the maximum constitutional extent (52-b as amended) — not labeled developer/deployer
choice_of_law_forum: personal jurisdiction in a civil action in this state to the maximum extent permitted under the U.S. Constitution and federal law (52-b); silent on choice of law
limitations_period: silent in the civil-rights sections as compiled in this pass
safe_harbor: Penal exceptions (LE/legal/medical; § 230); civil consent/First Amendment-adjacent limits as written
criminal_overlay: also crime — Penal L. § 245.15 class A misdemeanor; civil PRA in CRL 52-c/52-b
federal_preemption: cite — § 230 overlay as written in the penal/civil statutes; PJ to the maximum extent permitted under federal law
ai_definition: digitization: use of software, machine learning, artificial intelligence, or other computer-generated means, including adapting/modifying a realistic depiction (Part MM / 52-c)
summary: New York's civil intimate-image statutes reach images created or altered by digitization, including AI. CRL §§ 52-c and 52-b give the depicted person a PRA for injunction, compensatory and punitive damages, costs and fees. There is no BIPA-style liquidated schedule in those sections. Penal § 245.15 is a class A misdemeanor. No insurance carve-out.

citation_bill: Tex. Bus. & Com. Code ch. 552 (H.B. 149, 89th Leg., R.S., ch. 1174) — TRAIGA
short_title: Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act
who_regulated: Developers and deployers of AI systems offered/used in Texas; governmental entities (social scoring, biometric ID, consumer-facing disclosure); health-care service/treatment providers (AI disclosure)
hook: Intentional prohibited AI uses (self-harm/violence incitement; social scoring by government; biometric ID by government without consent; sole-intent constitutional infringement; intent to unlawfully discriminate; CSAM/NCII deepfakes; child-impersonating sexual chat). Consumer-facing government and health-care AI disclosure.
carve_outs: Ch. 552 may not be construed to authorize any agency other than TDI to regulate insurance. Unlawful-discrimination section does not apply to insurance entities providing insurance services if subject to unfair-discrimination / UTPA insurance statutes. Federally insured banks deemed compliant with that section if they comply with banking law. Disparate impact alone is not intent. Local AI ordinances preempted. No PRA.
enforcer: Attorney General exclusive (except licensed-person sanctions by a state agency after AG finding + recommendation, up to $100,000 plus license action). NIST GenAI RMF substantial compliance can defeat liability in specified circumstances.
private_suit: none (express)
statutory_damages: Civil penalties to the State: $10,000–$12,000 per curable violation or cure-statement breach; $80,000–$200,000 per uncurable violation; $2,000–$40,000 per day continuing. Not private damages.
cure_period: 60 days after AG written notice; AG may not sue if cured with supporting documentation and policy changes
class_collective: silent (no class language; chapter not subject to a PRA)
plaintiffs_together: none — chapter does not provide a basis for and is not subject to a private right of action (Bus. & Com. enrolled 552.106(b) family)
fee_shifting: yes — AG may recover attorney's fees and reasonable court costs (enrolled enforcement section)
notice_cure: 60 days after AG written notice identifying provisions alleged; AG may not sue before the 60th day if the person cures and documents the manner of cure plus policy changes (552.104)
nexus: subtitle applies only to a person who (1) promotes, advertises, or conducts business in this state; (2) produces a product or service used by residents of this state; or (3) develops or deploys an artificial intelligence system in this state (551.002). Consumer = resident of this state acting in an individual/household context. Deployer = deploys an AI system for use in this state; developer = develops an AI system offered/sold/leased/given/provided in this state (552.001).
out_of_state_actor: express — produces a product or service used by residents of this state, or develops/deploys an AI system in this state, or conducts business in this state (551.002)
insurance_situs: n/a (chapter may not be construed to authorize any agency other than TDI to regulate insurance; discrimination section inapplicable to insurance entities already under unfair-discrimination/UTPA insurance statutes)
safe_harbor: NIST GenAI RMF substantial compliance can defeat liability in specified circumstances (chapter as indexed); 60-day cure
local_preemption: yes — chapter supersedes and preempts any ordinance, resolution, rule, or other regulation adopted by a political subdivision regarding the use of AI systems (552.003)
ai_definition: AI system: any machine-based system that, for any explicit or implicit objective, infers from the inputs the system receives how to generate outputs, including content, decisions, predictions, or recommendations, that can influence physical or virtual environments (551.001)
impact_assessment_discoverable: silent (no IA mandate in TRAIGA as a high-risk assessment statute)
summary: TRAIGA, in force 1 Jan 2026, is a prohibition-and-disclosure statute, not a high-risk impact-assessment regime. It bars developing or deploying AI with specified bad intents, requires government (and certain health-care) AI-interaction disclosures, and gives the AG exclusive enforcement after a 60-day cure, with tiered civil penalties. Insurance entities are carved out of the discrimination section when already under insurance unfair-trade statutes, and the chapter does not authorize non-TDI agencies to regulate insurance. There is no private right of action.

citation_bill: Tex. Penal Code § 21.165; Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code ch. 98B (as amended by S.B. 441, 89th Leg., eff. 2025-09-01)
short_title: Unlawful production/distribution of deep fake intimate media; civil liability for artificial intimate visual material
operative_date: same; civil amendments apply to causes accruing on or after that date
who_regulated: Persons who produce or electronically distribute nonconsensual deep-fake intimate media; owners of sites/apps/nudification tools/payment processors in specified reckless-facilitation scenarios
hook: AI/ML deep fake media depicting a real person in intimate/sexual conduct that did not occur; civil 'artificial intimate visual material'
carve_outs: Affirmative defenses: law enforcement / reporting / legal proceedings; mere technical intermediaries; publicly accessible AI providers that prohibit NCII in terms, require user acknowledgment, and take listed technological steps. Written plain-language consent required for valid consent to produce/distribute.
enforcer: Criminal prosecutors (Class A misdemeanor; F3 if prior or depicted person <18). Private civil plaintiffs under ch. 98B. AG may seek injunction against repeat site/app notice/takedown violations; those subsections are also DTPA-actionable.
private_suit: PRA (ch. 98B)
statutory_damages: No fixed per-image liquidated sum in § 98B.003: prevailing claimant shall be awarded actual damages (including mental anguish), costs, and reasonable attorney's fees, and may recover exemplary damages. Separate $1,000 / $500 per violation of a court's 98B injunction. 72-hour takedown after request for site owners under § 98B.0022(b).
cure_period: 72 hours for website/app owners to remove material after the depicted person's request (§ 98B.0022(b)); not a general pre-suit cure
fee_shifting: yes — prevailing claimant shall be awarded costs and reasonable attorney's fees (98B.003 as amended)
notice_cure: 72 hours for website/app owners to remove material after the depicted person's request (§ 98B.0022(b)); not a general pre-suit cure
nexus: silent as a residence clause in the enrolled civil chapter (depicts a real person; Texas courts via CPRC)
retroactivity: civil amendments apply to causes accruing on or after 2025-09-01
limitations_period: suit not later than 10 years after the later of the date the depicted person reasonably discovers the intimate visual material, or turns 18 (98B.009 as amended by S.B. 441)
safe_harbor: affirmative defenses: LE/reporting/legal proceedings; mere technical intermediaries; publicly accessible AI providers that prohibit NCII in terms, require user acknowledgment, and take listed technological steps (S.B. 441)
criminal_overlay: also crime — Penal Code § 21.165 Class A misdemeanor (F3 if prior or depicted person <18); plus civil ch. 98B
ai_definition: deep fake media / artificial intimate visual material: AI/ML or computer-generated depiction of a real person in intimate/sexual conduct that did not occur (Penal § 21.165; CPRC ch. 98B)
summary: S.B. 441 expands Penal Code § 21.165 to AI deep-fake intimate media (production or electronic distribution without effective written consent) and threats to do so, with restitution on conviction. Chapter 98B adds civil liability for producing/soliciting/disclosing/promoting artificial intimate visual material with intent to harm, plus site/app/nudification/payment-processor theories and a 72-hour takedown duty. Civil recoveries are actual damages (including mental anguish), fees, and exemplary damages — not a BIPA-style $1k/$5k schedule.

citation_bill: Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 47-25-1101–1108 (ELVIS Act, 2024 Tenn. Pub. Acts ch. 588, HB 2091 / SB 2096)
short_title: Ensuring Likeness, Voice, and Image Security Act of 2024
who_regulated: Persons who use an individual's name, photograph, voice, or likeness; persons who publish/distribute unauthorized voice/likeness; persons who distribute a tool whose primary purpose is producing a particular identifiable individual's photograph, voice, or likeness
hook: Voice defined to include a readily identifiable simulation of an individual's voice (AI voice clones); commercial advertising/fundraising uses and knowing distribution of clone tools
carve_outs: Fair-use style exceptions in the 2024 amendments: news/public affairs/sports; comment, criticism, scholarship, satire, parody; self-portrayal in an audiovisual work unless it creates a false authentic-performance impression; fleeting/incidental use; ads for those excepted works. First Amendment overlay is express.
enforcer: Private civil action; Class A misdemeanor for unauthorized use; contraband seizure for tangible goods
private_suit: PRA
statutory_damages: No general liquidated sum: actual damages plus profits attributable to the use not taken into account in actual damages; injunction and destruction. Treble the (d)(1) amount plus reasonable attorney's fees if the knowing violation is of a member of the armed forces. (Secondary sources sometimes overstate general treble damages; the Justia compilation of § 47-25-1106(d)(2) limits treble+fees to armed-forces victims.)
plaintiffs_together: individual or, where a person has an exclusive recording-artist services contract or exclusive sound-recording distribution license, that person or the individual may sue (§ 47-25-1106(f) as added); silent on class
fee_shifting: yes, limited — treble the (d)(1) amount plus reasonable attorney's fees if the knowing violation is of a member of the armed forces (§ 47-25-1106(d)(2)); silent as a general fee-shift for other plaintiffs
nexus: silent (property right in name/photograph/voice/likeness in any medium in any manner; no in-state hook in Pub. Ch. 588)
retroactivity: effective 2024-07-01; silent as to pre-effective uses
safe_harbor: First Amendment fair-use list (news/public affairs/sports; comment/criticism/scholarship/satire/parody; self-portrayal unless false authentic-performance impression; fleeting/incidental; ads for those works) (§ 47-25-1107 as amended)
criminal_overlay: also crime — unauthorized use remains a Class A misdemeanor (cross-cite 39-14-152 family / existing publicity criminal overlay)
federal_preemption: cite — fair use to the extent protected by the First Amendment; audiovisual work defined under 17 U.S.C. § 101
ai_definition: n/a as AI/ADS — voice includes a sound readily identifiable and attributable to a particular individual regardless of whether it contains the actual voice or a simulation of the voice (Pub. Ch. 588 §3)
summary: The ELVIS Act renames Tennessee's publicity statute and extends the property right to voice, including simulated voice. Unauthorized commercial use, unauthorized publication/distribution of a voice or likeness, and distribution of a tool whose primary purpose is producing a particular person's voice/likeness, with knowledge of non-authorization, are civilly actionable and a Class A misdemeanor. Remedies are injunction, actual damages, and attributable profits; treble damages plus fees are statutory for knowing violations involving service members.

citation_bill: Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 39-17-1901–1906 (Preventing Deepfake Images Act, 2025 Tenn. Pub. Acts ch. 466, SB 1346 / HB 1299)
short_title: Preventing Deepfake Images Act
who_regulated: Persons who intentionally disclose an intimate digital depiction without consent, knowing or recklessly disregarding lack of consent (criminal track also covers threaten to disclose or solicit disclosure). Depicted individual identifiable by face, likeness, distinguishing characteristic, or accompanying information.
hook: Intimate-image AI deepfake: videos, images, or audio generated or manipulated by artificial intelligence to realistically portray something that did not occur (§ 39-17-1902); civil PRA plus Class E / Class C felony
carve_outs: No insurance/GLBA carve-out. Civil exceptions: good-faith disclosure to/by law enforcement investigating unlawful or unwelcome conduct; as part of a legal proceeding; or reasonably intended to assist the depicted individual (§ 39-17-1904(d)). ICS / information / telecommunications services not liable for good-faith restriction or content provided by another person (§§ 39-17-1905, 39-17-1906(d)). Disclaimer that the depiction is fake is not a defense. Consent to creation is not consent to disclosure; valid consent is a plain-language signed written agreement.
enforcer: Private civil plaintiffs. Criminal prosecutors (Class E felony default; Class C if the depiction could reasonably be expected to affect a governmental proceeding including administration of an election, or facilitate violence).
private_suit: PRA
statutory_damages: § 39-17-1904: (1) disgorgement of monetary gain from creation/development/disclosure; (2) either actual damages including emotional distress or liquidated $150,000; (3) punitive damages under § 29-39-104; (4) costs and reasonable attorney's fees. Equitable relief (TRO/prelim/permanent injunction); pseudonymous plaintiff. Not a public-penalty statute.
fee_shifting: yes — costs and reasonable attorney's fees (§ 39-17-1904)
nexus: silent as a residence clause (identifiable depicted individual; Tennessee criminal/civil chapter)
safe_harbor: ICS / information / telecommunications services not liable for good-faith restriction or content provided by another; civil LE/legal/assist-depicted exceptions (§§ 39-17-1904(d), 1905, 1906(d))
criminal_overlay: also crime — Class E felony default; Class C if the depiction could reasonably be expected to affect a governmental proceeding including administration of an election, or facilitate violence
ai_definition: intimate digital depiction includes videos, images, or audio generated or manipulated by artificial intelligence to realistically portray something that did not occur (§ 39-17-1902)
summary: Tennessee's 2025 intimate-deepfake statute creates a civil PRA for nonconsensual disclosure of an intimate digital depiction, defined to include AI-generated or AI-manipulated video, image, or audio of a real identifiable person. The plaintiff may recover disgorgement plus the greater of actual damages (including emotional distress) or $150,000 liquidated, punitive damages, and fees, with no cure period and no insurance or GLBA carve-out. A fake-disclaimer is not a defense. Criminal liability is a Class E felony, elevated to Class C in specified circumstances including effects on an election.

citation_bill: Tenn. Code Ann. § 2-19-120(a)(6) (Transparency for Deepfakes in Political Advertising Act, 2026 Tenn. Pub. Acts ch. 625, HB 1513 / SB 1624)
short_title: Transparency for Deepfakes in Political Advertising Act
who_regulated: Persons making an expenditure for a § 2-19-120 communication (express advocacy / contribution solicitation in general public political advertising) that is a deepfake impersonating or depicting a candidate engaging in speech or action that did not occur. Audio: spoken disclaimer at beginning and end. Video: on-screen large-letter disclaimer for the duration.
hook: Election / political deepfake disclosure (not a total ban); 'deepfake' imported from § 39-17-1902
carve_outs: No insurance/GLBA carve-out. Hosts, third-party producers, ISPs (including affiliates/subsidiaries), search engines, and cloud providers not liable solely for access/connection/transmission/caching if not responsible for creation of the deepfake. Radio/TV, cable/satellite, streaming/programming services paid to broadcast the material are not liable to the extent they did not create the deepfake. 120-day window before voting begins applies only when the impersonated/depicted candidate is not an incumbent.
enforcer: Class C misdemeanor via existing § 2-19-120(c) (district attorney). Depicted/impersonated candidate has a civil action.
private_suit: PAG (candidates depicted/impersonated only)
statutory_damages: Imports § 39-17-1904 civil menu except (c) (anonymity): disgorgement; actual damages including emotional distress or liquidated $150,000; punitive damages; costs and fees; equitable relief. No independent liquidated schedule in ch. 625 itself.
plaintiffs_together: PAG — depicted/impersonated candidate only; imports § 39-17-1904 civil menu except anonymity (c)
fee_shifting: yes — imported 1904 costs and reasonable attorney's fees
nexus: expenditure for a § 2-19-120 communication (express advocacy / contribution solicitation in general public political advertising) that is a deepfake; 120-day window before voting begins applies only when the impersonated/depicted candidate is not an incumbent (PC 625)
safe_harbor: hosts, third-party producers, ISPs (incl. affiliates), search engines, and cloud providers not liable solely for access/connection/transmission/caching if not responsible for creation; paid radio/TV/cable/satellite/streaming not liable to the extent they did not create the deepfake
criminal_overlay: also crime — Class C misdemeanor via existing § 2-19-120(c); plus candidate civil action
ai_definition: deepfake imported from § 39-17-1902 (AI-generated or manipulated intimate-depiction definition used for the political-ad disclaimer)
summary: Effective 1 Jul 2026, Tennessee requires a deepfake disclaimer on specified political advertising that impersonates or depicts a candidate in speech or action that did not occur. The impersonated or depicted candidate is entitled to damages and equitable relief as provided in § 39-17-1904, except the anonymity subsection (c) — so the intimate-deepfake civil menu, including $150,000 liquidated or actual, is imported into election-ad cases. Hosts and paid broadcasters who did not create the deepfake are carved out. There is no insurance/GLBA carve-out and no cure period. Violation of the host political-disclaimer statute remains a Class C misdemeanor.

citation_bill: Utah Code tit. 13, ch. 77 (SB 226, 2025 Gen. Sess. ch. 465; later amended ch. 95, 2026); originally SB 149 (2024) at former § 13-2-12
short_title: Generative Artificial Intelligence — Consumer Disclosures and Enforcement
who_regulated: Suppliers using GenAI in consumer transactions; individuals providing services in Department of Commerce-regulated occupations (includes licensed insurance producers as a regulated occupation)
hook: GenAI that simulates human conversation (text/audio/visual) with limited human oversight; high-risk interactions involving health/financial/biometric data or personalized financial, legal, medical, or mental-health advice
carve_outs: UCSPA 'consumer transaction' expressly excepts securities and insurance (Utah Code § 13-11-3(2)(a)) — selling an insurance policy is generally not a ch. 77 consumer-transaction chatbot event. The licensed/certified-occupation high-risk disclosure (13-77-103(2)) is NOT limited to consumer transactions and can still reach Commerce-licensed insurance producers. Supplier disclosure is only on a clear and unambiguous human-vs-AI prompt. Safe harbor if GenAI discloses at the outset and throughout (13-77-104). B2B that is not a UCSPA consumer transaction is out.
enforcer: Division of Consumer Protection; AG as counsel. Violation is also a Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act violation (13-11-4(1)).
private_suit: none (AG/DCP only; no PRA in ch. 77)
statutory_damages: Administrative fine up to $2,500 per violation; court fine up to $2,500 per violation in a Division action; civil penalty up to $5,000 per violation of an administrative or court order. Not a private liquidated-damages PRA.
cure_period: none in ch. 77 (safe harbor is disclosure-based, not a cure period)
plaintiffs_together: none (DCP/AG only; no PRA in ch. 77)
notice_cure: silent (none in ch. 77; safe harbor is disclosure-based)
nexus: UCSPA consumer transaction (which excepts insurance/securities under § 13-11-3(2)(a)); licensed-occupation high-risk disclosure is not limited to consumer transactions
insurance_situs: n/a for the consumer-transaction chatbot duty (insurance excepted); licensed insurance producers can still face the high-risk occupation disclosure — situs of a policy silent
safe_harbor: yes — 13-77-104: not subject to an enforcement action for violating 13-77-103 if the person's GenAI clearly and conspicuously discloses at the outset and throughout that the user is interacting with AI
ai_definition: generative artificial intelligence defined in 13-77-101 (conversational GenAI that simulates human conversation with limited human oversight — read 13-77-101 for the full compiled definition)
summary: Utah ch. 77 requires a supplier using conversational GenAI in a UCSPA consumer transaction to disclose that the counterparty is not human if the individual clearly and unambiguously asks. That consumer-transaction duty excepts insurance and securities under § 13-11-3(2)(a). Licensed occupations must proactively disclose GenAI in high-risk interactions (including financial/insurance-adjacent advice). The Division may fine up to $2,500 per violation; there is no consumer PRA.

citation_bill: Utah Code tit. 13, ch. 72 (SB 149 (2024); sunset extended by SB 332 (2025) to 2027-07-01; HB 320 (2026) program amendments)
short_title: Utah Artificial Intelligence Policy Act — Office of AI Policy / Learning Laboratory
operative_date: Office/Lab currently operative; Chapter 72 repeal date 2027-07-01 per 2025 extension (confirm 2026 HB 320 did not move that date)
who_regulated: Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy; Learning Lab participants seeking regulatory mitigation / joint interpretation agreements

enforcer: Office of AI Policy / Division as provided in ch. 72
private_suit: none

nexus: silent (state office/sandbox)
retroactivity: office/lab; Chapter 72 repeal date 2027-07-01 per 2025 extension
safe_harbor: sandbox mitigations are participant-specific joint-interpretation/regulatory-mitigation agreements — not a general private-sector harbor

summary: SB 149 created the Office of AI Policy and a Learning Laboratory that can grant time-limited regulatory mitigations. SB 332 extended the Chapter 72 repeal to 1 Jul 2027; 2026 amendments added joint-interpretation agreements. This chapter is the sandbox/office, not the consumer disclosure duty (now Chapter 77). Treat the 1 Jul 2027 date as a statutory sunset of the office/lab unless the Legislature extends it.

short_title: Artificial Intelligence Applications Relating to Mental Health
who_regulated: Suppliers of mental-health chatbots used by a Utah user (individual located in Utah at time of use)
hook: GenAI chatbot that a supplier represents, or a reasonable person would believe, can provide mental-health therapy or help manage/treat mental-health conditions
carve_outs: Scripted-only tools (e.g., guided meditations) and tools that only analyze input to connect the user to a human therapist are outside the definition (as described in official-adjacent bill analyses; confirm § 13-72a-101). No ch. 72 sunset on this chapter.
enforcer: Division of Consumer Protection; AG as counsel. 58-60-118 is an affirmative defense to unlicensed-practice charges, not a PRA.
private_suit: none (DCP/AG-only; no PRA in ch. 72a)
statutory_damages: Same DCP stack as ch. 77: administrative fine up to $2,500 per violation; court fine up to $2,500; order-violation up to $5,000. Not a private liquidated-damages PRA.
nexus: suppliers of mental-health chatbots used by a Utah user (individual located in Utah at time of use)
out_of_state_actor: silent (hook is use by an individual located in Utah at time of use)
safe_harbor: scripted-only tools and tools that only connect the user to a human therapist are outside the definition (confirm § 13-72a-101)
criminal_overlay: civil-only (58-60-118 is an affirmative defense to unlicensed-practice charges, not a PRA)
ai_definition: GenAI chatbot that a supplier represents, or a reasonable person would believe, can provide mental-health therapy or help manage/treat mental-health conditions (ch. 72a)
summary: Utah regulates mental-health chatbots offered to users physically located in the state. A covered chatbot must disclose that it is AI before first access, after a seven-day gap, and whenever the user asks. Enforcement is DCP/AG; there is no private right of action in chapter 72a. Penalties track the $2,500 / $5,000 Division stack.

citation_bill: Utah Code § 31A-22-650 as amended (SB 319, 2026 Gen. Sess., ch. 240 as commonly cited)
short_title: Health insurance preauthorization — AI disclosure and human medical judgment
who_regulated: Health insurers subject to Utah Insurance Code preauthorization rules that use AI in reviewing authorization requests
hook: AI in prior-authorization / authorization-request review; independent medical judgment on clinical/medical-necessity denials
carve_outs: Special effective date 2027-01-01. Prescription-drug timing carve-outs appear in bill summaries — confirm in the enrolled bill. Not a GLBA privacy statute.
enforcer: Utah Insurance Department (existing Insurance Code tools; SB 319 does not appear to add a new PRA)
private_suit: none identified in bill summaries; unconfirmed from enrolled text
statutory_damages: none identified in SB 319; unconfirmed
fee_shifting: silent (unconfirmed from enrolled as a new fee-shift)
nexus: silent (health insurers subject to Utah Insurance Code preauthorization rules)
insurance_situs: silent (no delivered/issued clause identified in SB 319 as indexed)
criminal_overlay: silent (expected Insurance Department civil/admin tools; no new PRA identified)
ai_definition: AI in reviewing authorization requests; adverse clinical/medical-necessity determinations must be by an individual exercising independent medical judgment (SB 319)
