Adverse clinical/medical-necessity determinations must be made by an individual exercising independent medical judgment, not solely on another source's (including AI) recommendation. Enforcement is expected to ride existing Insurance Department authority; a new PRA was not identified.

citation_bill: Utah Code § 20A-11-1104 (SB 131, 2024 Gen. Sess.)
short_title: Election synthetic-media disclosure
who_regulated: Creator (person who uses AI to generate synthetic media; not a mere tech provider) and sponsor (person who pays) of a paid audio/visual communication intended to influence voting for/against a candidate or ballot proposition in a Utah election/primary, paid by a candidate committee, PAC, PIC, party, or person using a contribution, that contains synthetic media
hook: Election / political deepfake disclosure
carve_outs: Creator excludes sole technology providers. No insurance/GLBA carve-out.
enforcer: A person may bring a civil action against creator or sponsor
private_suit: PRA (civil penalty)
statutory_damages: Civil penalty not to exceed $1,000 per violation. Compliance does not exempt other civil/criminal liability.
plaintiffs_together: PRA — a person may bring a civil action against creator or sponsor (20A-11-1104); silent on class
nexus: paid audio/visual communication intended to influence voting for/against a candidate or ballot proposition in a Utah election/primary
criminal_overlay: civil-only as this section (compliance does not exempt other civil/criminal liability)
ai_definition: synthetic media created using AI (20A-11-1104); creator = person who uses AI to generate synthetic media, not a mere tech provider
summary: Utah requires specified paid political audio/visual communications that contain AI synthetic media to carry labeled disclosures (and online ads, tamper-evident provenance). A person may sue the creator or sponsor for a civil penalty not to exceed $1,000 per violation. Mere technology providers are not 'creators.'

citation_bill: Utah Code tit. 13, ch. 72b (Digital Voyeurism Prevention Act) as enacted by HB 276, 2026 Gen. Sess. (same bill also enacts ch. 72c provenance, AG-only, not a separate index row)
short_title: Digital Voyeurism Prevention Act
operative_date: 2027-01-01 (capture-device latent-disclosure in companion ch. 72c: devices produced for sale in Utah on or after 2028-01-01)
who_regulated: Generation services (server-side intimate-image generators) and covered platforms (Take It Down Act definition)
hook: Intimate-image AI generation / NCII deepfake (platforms and generation services)
carve_outs: Safe harbors and heightened pleading for generation services and platforms; § 230 savings; Take It Down Act alignment. No insurance/GLBA carve-out.
enforcer: Private plaintiffs (13-72b). Companion 13-72c provenance duties are DCP/AG-only.
private_suit: PRA (13-72b). 13-72c in the same bill is AG-only.
statutory_damages: 13-72b: injunction, destruction, actual damages including emotional distress, punitive if willful/reckless/malicious, fees. Damages need not be proved to get injunction/destruction. No general liquidated dollar floor. Platform takedown: 48 hours after qualifying notice.
cure_period: 48-hour platform takedown after qualifying notice (not a general pre-suit cure)
plaintiffs_together: PRA against generation services and covered platforms (13-72b); silent on class
fee_shifting: yes — fees among 13-72b remedies (injunction, destruction, actual incl. emotional distress, punitive if willful, fees)
notice_cure: 48-hour platform takedown after qualifying notice (not a general pre-suit cure)
nexus: silent as a general residence clause in the indexed row (generation services / Take It Down covered platforms; confirm enrolled HB 276 for any Utah-user hook)
retroactivity: most sections 2027-01-01; capture-device latent-disclosure companion ch. 72c: devices produced for sale in Utah on or after 2028-01-01
limitations_period: silent in the enrolled materials as indexed
safe_harbor: safe harbors and heightened pleading for generation services and platforms; § 230 savings; Take It Down Act alignment (HB 276)
federal_preemption: cite — § 230 savings; Take It Down Act alignment (HB 276)
ai_definition: intimate-image AI generation / NCII deepfake as defined in 13-72b (read enrolled HB 276 for the generation-service definition)
summary: HB 276 (signed 24 Mar 2026, most sections 1 Jan 2027) creates a PRA against intimate-image generation services and covered platforms (13-72b): injunction, destruction, actual damages including emotional distress, and punitive damages if willful. The same bill's provenance chapter (13-72c) is AG-only and is not a separate row. This is a real AI/NCII statute, not yet operative.

short_title: Unlawful dissemination or sale of images of another (NCII / deepfake images)
enacted_date: Deepfake 'another person' definition: 2019; 2024 c. 697 further amendment
effective_date: In force (2024 amendment effective per that chapter — typically 2024-07-01)
who_regulated: Persons who maliciously disseminate or sell nude/undress/obscene images of another, including AI-adapted images of a recognizable actual person, with intent to coerce, harass, or intimidate, knowing they are not authorized
hook: Videographic or still image created by any means, including creating/adapting/modifying an image to depict a recognizable actual person
carve_outs: Internet/email/information service providers not responsible for content provided by another person. Does not preclude other prosecutions.
enforcer: Criminal prosecutors (Class 1 misdemeanor)
private_suit: none in this section
statutory_damages: none in this section (criminal fine schedule for Class 1 misdemeanor is not a civil statutory-damages PRA)
nexus: silent as a residence clause in § 18.2-386.2 (malicious dissemination/sale of images of another)
limitations_period: silent (criminal limitations are outside this section)
safe_harbor: internet/email/information service providers not responsible for content provided by another person
criminal_overlay: also crime — Class 1 misdemeanor; this section is criminal only (no civil PRA)
ai_definition: videographic or still image created by any means, including creating/adapting/modifying an image to depict a recognizable actual person (another person includes that individual)
summary: Virginia's NCII statute reaches images created by any means and expressly treats as 'another person' someone whose image was used to create, adapt, or modify a depiction of an actual recognizable person — covering AI intimate deepfakes. The offense is a Class 1 misdemeanor when done maliciously with intent to coerce, harass, or intimidate and without authorization. ISPs are not liable for others' content. This section is criminal only; it does not create a civil PRA.

citation_bill: Va. Code §§ 59.1-575–59.1-585 (VCDPA, 2021 cc.; later minor amendments). Included only for the ADS/profiling hook.
short_title: Virginia Consumer Data Protection Act — profiling opt-out and assessments
who_regulated: Controllers meeting VCDPA thresholds (100,000 VA consumers, or 25,000 plus data-sale revenue test)
hook: Right to opt out of profiling in furtherance of decisions that produce legal or similarly significant effects; data-protection assessments for that profiling
carve_outs: GLBA financial institutions and data; HIPAA; several other VCDPA entity/data exemptions. Not an insurance unfair-discrimination AI testing statute. No PRA.
enforcer: Attorney General exclusive
private_suit: none
statutory_damages: none (AG civil penalties under VCDPA — up to $7,500 per violation is the commonly quoted figure; confirm § 59.1-584 before relying)
cure_period: 30-day cure in VCDPA (still in the Act as commonly compiled; confirm current § 59.1-584)
class_collective: silent (no class language; exclusive AG enforcement / no PRA)
plaintiffs_together: none — nothing in this chapter shall be construed as providing the basis for, or be subject to, a private right of action for violations of this chapter or under any other law (§ 59.1-584(E))
fee_shifting: yes — AG may recover reasonable expenses including attorney fees (§ 59.1-584(D)); collected amounts to a state fund
notice_cure: 30 days written notice identifying provisions; if cured within 30 days with an express written statement that violations have been cured and no further violations shall occur, no action shall be initiated (§ 59.1-584(B))
nexus: persons that conduct business in the Commonwealth or produce products or services that are targeted to residents of the Commonwealth and that meet the volume/revenue tests (§ 59.1-576(A)); consumer = natural person who is a resident of the Commonwealth acting in an individual or household context (§ 59.1-575)
out_of_state_actor: express — produce products or services that are targeted to residents of the Commonwealth (§ 59.1-576(A))
insurance_situs: n/a (GLBA FI/data exempt; profiling legal or similarly significant effects definition includes insurance as a decision type — not an insurance-code situs rule)
thresholds: during a calendar year, control or process personal data of at least 100,000 consumers, or of at least 25,000 consumers and derive over 50 percent of gross revenue from the sale of personal data (§ 59.1-576(A))
safe_harbor: 30-day cure if the written statement is given (§ 59.1-584(B))
federal_preemption: silent (GLBA/HIPAA and other federal-scheme exemptions are entity/data carve-outs, not a preemption clause)
ai_definition: profiling in furtherance of decisions that produce legal or similarly significant effects (provision/denial of financial/lending, housing, insurance, education, criminal justice, employment, health care, or basic necessities) (§ 59.1-575) — not an AI definition
impact_assessment_discoverable: silent in §§ 575/576/584 as pulled (assessments required for that profiling under 59.1-580; quote 59.1-580 for confidentiality before treating as discoverable or not)
summary: Virginia has no enacted comprehensive high-risk AI act (HB 2094 was vetoed 24 Mar 2025; override failed). The VCDPA is a general privacy law, indexed here only because it gives consumers an opt-out of profiling for legal or similarly significant effects and requires assessments for that processing. GLBA-regulated institutions are outside. The AG enforces; there is no PRA. Do not treat VCDPA as a Colorado-style AI act.

citation_bill: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 6, § 220 (St. 2020, c. 253, police-reform package)
short_title: Law enforcement facial recognition searches
effective_date: in force (c. 253 effective clauses; § 220 is current G.L. text)
who_regulated: Law enforcement agencies performing or requesting a facial recognition search; RMV, Department of State Police, and FBI as the only search channels named
hook: Government use / biometric AI: facial recognition searches by law enforcement only through written request to RMV, State Police, or FBI, and only with a court/warrant-issuer order (reasonable grounds) or without an order to identify a deceased person or in a documented emergency involving substantial risk of harm
carve_outs: Agencies may acquire personal devices that use facial recognition solely for user authentication, and automated video/image redaction software that cannot perform facial recognition or other remote biometric recognition. Evidence from a biometric surveillance system is restricted if the system was knowingly solicited in violation of (b).
enforcer: No private enforcer named in § 220; limits law-enforcement search practice (court order / emergency documentation)
private_suit: none in this section
statutory_damages: none in this section
nexus: silent as a residence clause (Massachusetts law-enforcement searches / RMV-DSP-FBI channel)
safe_harbor: device authentication and non-FR redaction software; emergency search with documented factual basis
criminal_overlay: civil-only as this section (search limits / evidentiary restriction; not a consumer crime)
federal_preemption: silent (FBI named as a permitted search channel, not a preemption clause)
ai_definition: facial recognition search / facial recognition technology / biometric surveillance system (terms as used in § 220; no general AI definition)
record_retention: emergency requests shall document the factual basis; other documentation duties in § 220
summary: Section 220 confines Massachusetts law-enforcement facial-recognition searches to written requests routed through RMV, State Police, or the FBI, and only for a court-authorized criminal investigation or a documented emergency/decedent identification. It is a government-use biometric statute, not a private-sector AI act. No PRA, statutory damages, or insurance-code hook.

citation_bill: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 265, § 43A(b) (St. 2024, c. 118, An Act to prevent abuse and exploitation)
short_title: Criminal harassment — nonconsensual intimate images including digitization/deepfakes
effective_date: 2024-09-18 (90 days after signing; Mass.gov LE summary of c. 118)
who_regulated: Whoever knowingly distributes visual material, including material produced by digitization, depicting an identifiable person who is nude, partially nude, or engaged in sexual conduct, causing physical or economic injury or substantial emotional distress
hook: Deepfake / intimate synthetic media: digitization is creation or alteration of visual material, including computer-generated images, in a manner that would falsely appear to a reasonable person to be an authentic representation of the person depicted
carve_outs: Does not apply to voluntary/consensual nudity in a commercial setting or where there is no reasonable expectation of privacy; public-interest reporting of unlawful conduct; lawful LE/corrections/legal/medical (incl. telemedicine) practices; matter of public concern; ICS as defined in 47 U.S.C. § 230(f)(2) and information/telecommunications services as defined in 47 U.S.C. § 153 for content solely provided by another. Consent to creation is not consent to distribution.
enforcer: Criminal prosecutors (criminal harassment). Subsection (b)(4) preserves other remedies at law or in equity, including restraining orders against distribution — not a liquidated civil PRA.
private_suit: none in this subsection (other remedies including injunction expressly not precluded; no statutory civil cause with scheduled damages)
statutory_damages: none as private liquidated damages. Criminal: house of correction ≤ 2½ years and/or fine ≤ $10,000 for the (b) distribution offense; first-offense criminal-harassment fine otherwise raised to $5,000; subsequent up to $15,000 / state prison 10 years under (c)
nexus: silent as a residence clause (distribution of visual material of another)
limitations_period: silent in c. 118 for this offense (c. 118 separately extended SOL for other c. 265 family-violence crimes)
safe_harbor: ICS 47 U.S.C. § 230(f)(2) and telecom/information services 47 U.S.C. § 153 for content solely provided by another; LE/legal/medical/public-concern/commercial-exposure exceptions
criminal_overlay: also crime — criminal harassment; does not preclude prosecution under G.L. c. 272 § 29C
federal_preemption: silent (47 U.S.C. §§ 230/153 are safe-harbor cross-cites, not a preemption clause)
ai_definition: digitization: creation or alteration of visual material including through computer-generated images so it would falsely appear to a reasonable person to be an authentic representation of the person depicted (§ 43A(b)(1))
record_retention: court-record visual material in a (b) prosecution is not open to public inspection except as specified
summary: Chapter 118 added G.L. c. 265 § 43A(b), making knowing distribution of intimate visual material — including computer-generated/digitized deepfakes that a reasonable person would take as authentic — criminal harassment (up to 2½ years and/or $10,000). No statutory liquidated PRA; other injunctive/equitable remedies are preserved. Massachusetts has no enacted election-deepfake statute, no insurance-code AI UR statute, and no BIPA-style biometric damages statute as of 2026-09-02.

citation_bill: Md. Code Ann., Com. Law §§ 14-4601–14-4614 (Maryland Online Data Privacy Act of 2024, SB 541, 2024 Md. Laws ch. 455)
short_title: Maryland Online Data Privacy Act (profiling / ADS hook)
operative_date: in force; § 14-4612 processing activities only prospective as to activities before 2026-04-01 (ch. 455 § 2)
who_regulated: Controllers/processors that conduct business in Maryland or provide products/services targeted to residents of the State and that, in the preceding calendar year, controlled or processed personal data of ≥35,000 consumers (excluding data solely to complete a payment) or ≥10,000 consumers and derived >20% of gross revenue from the sale of personal data
hook: ADS / profiling inside a privacy code: consumer right to opt out of profiling in furtherance of solely automated decisions that produce legal or similarly significant effects (definition expressly includes provision or denial of insurance); DPIA required for profiling that presents reasonably foreseeable unfair/abusive/deceptive treatment, unlawful disparate impact, financial/physical/reputational injury, offensive intrusion, or other substantial injury. Sensitive data includes biometric data generated by automatic measurements of biological characteristics.
carve_outs: Entity: State/local government bodies; certain SEC/CFTC associations; a financial institution, affiliate, or data subject to GLBA Title V; limited nonprofit LE/first-responder processors. Data: HIPAA PHI; specified research/human-subjects; FCRA and other standard data exemptions; personal data collected for, provided to, or used by or on behalf of a person regulated under the Insurance Article or an affiliate, in furtherance of the business of insurance (§ 14-4603(B)(13)).
enforcer: Division of Consumer Protection (Attorney General) via Title 13 of the Commercial Law Article, except § 13-408 (the Title 13 private action is carved out of MODPA enforcement)
private_suit: none (violation is a Title 13 unfair/abusive/deceptive practice except § 13-408; § 14-4613(b) does not prevent other remedies provided by law — not a new MODPA PRA)
statutory_damages: none as private liquidated damages. Public Title 13 penalties apply (amounts in Title 13, not restated as a MODPA schedule)
cure_period: For alleged violations on or before 2027-04-01, the Division may issue a notice of violation if it determines a cure is possible; if issued, at least 60 days to cure (§ 14-4614). Discretionary, not a mandatory pre-suit cure.
notice_cure: Division may give ≥60-day cure for violations on or before 2027-04-01 if it determines a cure is possible (§ 14-4614)
nexus: conducts business in the State or provides products or services that are targeted to residents of the State, plus volume/sale thresholds (§ 14-4602)
out_of_state_actor: provides products or services that are targeted to residents of the State (paired with thresholds)
insurance_situs: n/a (Insurance Article data in furtherance of the business of insurance is a data exemption, not a situs test)
thresholds: ≥35,000 consumers (excluding payment-completion-only processing) or ≥10,000 consumers and >20% gross revenue from sale of personal data
retroactivity: § 14-4612 construed only prospectively; no effect on processing activities before 2026-04-01 (ch. 455 § 2)
safe_harbor: COPPA-compliant parental consent deemed compliance for child consent; GLBA/Insurance-Article data exemptions
federal_preemption: silent (GLBA, HIPAA, Airline Deregulation, COPPA are exemptions/safe harbors, not a general preemption clause)
ai_definition: no standalone AI definition. Profiling = any form of automated processing of personal data to evaluate, analyze, or predict economic situation, health, demographic characteristics, preferences, interests, reliability, behavior, location, or movements. Biometric data = data generated by automatic measurements of biological characteristics of a consumer that can be used to uniquely identify the consumer.
impact_assessment_discoverable: controller shall conduct and document, on a regular basis, a data protection assessment for heightened-risk processing including specified profiling (§ 14-4610); silent on private-party discovery
record_retention: silent as a year-count (assessments documented on a regular basis)
summary: MODPA is Maryland's comprehensive consumer privacy statute with an ADS hook: opt-out of solely automated profiling that produces legal or similarly significant effects (including insurance decisions) and DPIAs for risky profiling. Biometric data is sensitive. Enforcement is AG/Division Title 13 except the § 13-408 private action. GLBA entities/data and Insurance Article business-of-insurance data are out. No BIPA-style liquidated PRA.

citation_bill: Md. Code Ann., State Fin. & Proc. §§ 3.5-801–3.5-806 (Artificial Intelligence Governance Act of 2024, SB 818, 2024 Md. Laws ch. 496)
short_title: Artificial Intelligence Governance Act of 2024 (state-government high-risk AI)
operative_date: new high-risk AI deploy/procure ban beginning 2025-07-01 unless DoIT policies are met (§ 3.5-805); inventories/impact assessments on the chapter's staged dates
who_regulated: Units of State government (AG, Comptroller, Treasurer, and specified public higher-ed have compatible-policy tracks rather than identical DoIT control). Research/academic AI at public senior higher-ed and Baltimore City Community College is carved to a parallel policy/report track.
hook: Government use of high-risk / rights-impacting or safety-impacting AI: unit inventories, DoIT policies, impact assessments, and a bar on deploying a new AI system unless it complies with adopted policies
carve_outs: Public senior higher-education / BCCC research-or-academic-purpose AI is not under the main subtitle duties but must adopt functionally compatible policies and annual high-risk AI reports. Independent constitutional officers (AG, Comptroller, Treasurer) establish compatible policies.
enforcer: Department of Information Technology; Governor's Artificial Intelligence Subcabinet (policy/oversight). No consumer PRA.
private_suit: none
statutory_damages: none
nexus: units of State government (Maryland executive/IT subtitle)
retroactivity: new-system deploy bar 2025-07-01; not a general private-sector retroactivity clause
safe_harbor: research/academic higher-ed parallel track; constitutional-officer compatible policies
ai_definition: artificial intelligence: a machine-based system that (1) can, for a given set of human-defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations, or decisions influencing real or virtual environments; (2) uses machine and human-based inputs to perceive real and virtual environments and abstracts those perceptions into models through analysis in an automated manner; and (3) uses model inference to formulate options for information or action (SF&P § 3.5-801(c), as reprinted in 2026 ch. 445)
impact_assessment_discoverable: units shall conduct regular impact assessments of rights-impacting or safety-impacting high-risk AI as determined by the Subcabinet; inventories public as aggregated statewide inventory on DoIT's website (security withholdings apply)
record_retention: annual inventories and reports; no consumer year-count
summary: Chapter 496 is a state-government AI governance statute: inventories of high-risk AI, DoIT policies, impact assessments, and a 1 Jul 2025 bar on deploying new AI systems that do not comply. It does not regulate private-sector developers/deployers and creates no PRA.

citation_bill: Md. Code Ann., Crim. Proc. §§ 2-501–2-510 (SB 182, 2024 Md. Laws ch. 808)
short_title: Law enforcement facial recognition technology
who_regulated: Law enforcement agencies using or contracting for facial recognition technology in criminal investigations; officers/employees/agents authorized to use it
hook: Government use / biometric AI: facial recognition technology (computer program/service/technology that analyzes facial features for identification, verification, or persistent tracking in still or video images for criminal investigations). Results may not be sole probable cause; independent trained-human verification required; prohibited uses (personal interest, political/social beliefs, lawful activity, protected-class targeting); suppression of results generated in violation; annual public reporting.
carve_outs: Does not include technology used only to grant or deny access to an electronic device. Additional operational limits and database-contract conditions are in the subtitle.
enforcer: Law enforcement policy/training/reporting (Governor's Office of Crime Prevention receives annual reports). Evidentiary exclusion in criminal/juvenile proceedings for results generated in violation. No consumer PRA.
private_suit: none in this subtitle
statutory_damages: none in this subtitle
nexus: Maryland law-enforcement agencies (criminal investigations)
out_of_state_actor: silent (contracts for nongovernment FR systems must be disclosed on the agency website)
safe_harbor: device-unlock FR excluded from the definition; limited introduction of derived evidence if the court finds specified conditions
criminal_overlay: civil-only as this subtitle (procedure/evidence/reporting); not a new consumer crime
ai_definition: facial recognition technology: a computer program, service, or other technology that analyzes facial features and is used by or at the direction of a law enforcement agency for identification, verification, or persistent tracking of individuals in still or video images for use in criminal investigations (§ 2-501)
record_retention: annual reports by 1 Feb (agency publish) / 1 May (submit) / 1 Oct (statewide compilation)
summary: Chapter 808 regulates Maryland law-enforcement use of facial recognition: independent human verification, bans on specified discriminatory or off-duty uses, evidentiary limits, vendor disclosure, and annual demographic/use reporting. Government biometric AI, not a private-sector BIPA.

short_title: Health insurance utilization review — use of artificial intelligence
who_regulated: Carriers (insurer, nonprofit health service plan, HMO, dental plan organization, or other person that provides health benefit plans subject to State regulation) that use AI/algorithm/other software for utilization review or that contract through an entity that does; PBMs and private review agents that contract with a carrier to provide UR and use such tools
hook: Insurance-code AI: UR tools must base determinations on the enrollee's clinical history/circumstances/record, not solely on a group dataset; may not replace the health-care provider's role in the § 15-10B-07 determination process; no unfair discrimination; open to Commissioner audit; quarterly performance review; patient data not used beyond intended purpose (HIPAA as applicable). Express: an AI, algorithm, or other software tool may not deny, delay or modify health care services (§ 15-10B-05.1(D)). Adverse-decision quarterly reports must state whether such a tool was used.
carve_outs: No GLBA entity carve-out in this section (it is an Insurance Article UR duty). Scope is health-benefit UR, not P&C underwriting.
enforcer: Maryland Insurance Commissioner (audit/compliance; existing UR penalty machinery under Title 15 Subtitle 10B, including § 15-10B-11 as referenced in the amended reporting section)
private_suit: none in this chaptered text
statutory_damages: none in this chaptered text (no new consumer liquidated PRA)
nexus: carriers providing health benefit plans subject to regulation by the State; UR on behalf of those carriers
out_of_state_actor: silent (duty attaches to State-regulated carriers and their UR contractors)
insurance_situs: health benefit plans subject to regulation by the State; 15-10A-06 reporting is for members entitled under a policy, plan, or certificate issued or delivered in the State
federal_preemption: silent (HIPAA named as data-use consistency, not preemption of the UR rule)
ai_definition: artificial intelligence: an engineered or machine-based system that varies in its level of autonomy and that can, for explicit or implicit objectives, infer from the input it receives how to generate outputs that can influence physical or virtual environments (§ 15-10B-05.1(A)(2))
impact_assessment_discoverable: tool open to inspection for audit or compliance reviews by the Commissioner; quarterly review/revision of performance, use, and outcomes — not a public AIA
record_retention: written policies in the utilization plan under § 15-10B-05; quarterly performance review
summary: Chapter 747 is Maryland's insurance-code AI UR statute. Carriers, PBMs, and private review agents may not let an AI/algorithm/software tool deny, delay, or modify health care services; tools cannot replace the clinician's determination role, cannot decide solely from a group dataset, and must be auditable by the Commissioner. No new PRA. 2026 HB 1385 (human evaluation of AI UR) was not enacted.

citation_bill: Md. Code Ann., Crim. Law § 3-809; Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 3-505 (SB 360, 2025 Md. Laws ch. 219)
short_title: Revenge porn — computer-generated visual representation and civil action
who_regulated: Persons who knowingly distribute a visual representation of another identifiable person with intimate parts exposed or engaged in sexual activity (legacy elements), or who knowingly distribute a computer-generated visual representation indistinguishable from another actual and identifiable person displaying intimate parts or sexual activity, with intent to harm/harass/intimidate/threaten/coerce and knowledge or reckless disregard of lack of consent
hook: Intimate deepfake: computer-generated visual representation created with or without existing depictions, indistinguishable to an ordinary person from an actual visual representation; drawings/cartoons/sculptures/paintings excluded
carve_outs: Does not apply to lawful LE / reporting of unlawful conduct / legal proceedings, or voluntary exposure in public or commercial settings. ICS as defined in 47 U.S.C. § 230(f)(2) is not liable for content provided by another person.
enforcer: State's Attorney (criminal misdemeanor). Depicted person has a civil cause of action.
private_suit: PRA — CJP § 3-505 (defamation per se for CG distribution) and CL § 3-809(f) (defamation per se or invasion of privacy against any person who distributed the visual representation)
statutory_damages: no liquidated floor/cap in the chaptered text (defamation per se / invasion of privacy plus other relief; court may award reasonable attorney's fees to a prevailing plaintiff)
fee_shifting: yes — court may award reasonable attorney's fees to a prevailing plaintiff (CJP § 3-505(c); CL § 3-809(f)(2))
nexus: silent as a residence clause (distribution of a visual representation of another identifiable person)
limitations_period: silent in ch. 219 for the civil action (criminal timing rules of § 3-809 are outside the civil PRA)
safe_harbor: ICS 47 U.S.C. § 230(f)(2) for content provided by another; LE/legal/public-or-commercial-exposure exceptions
criminal_overlay: also crime — misdemeanor, imprisonment ≤ 2 years or fine ≤ $5,000 or both (§ 3-809(d)); plus civil PRA
ai_definition: computer-generated visual representation includes a representation created without using other existing visual representations of a person, or created using other existing visual representations without consent; indistinguishable-from-actual includes a CG representation created, adapted, or modified to appear genuine / as an actual identifiable person
record_retention: visual representations that are court records in a § 3-809 case are not open to public inspection except as listed (now including civil plaintiff/plaintiff's attorney)
summary: Chapter 219 extends Maryland revenge-porn law to computer-generated intimate images indistinguishable from an actual person and adds a civil action for defamation per se (CJP § 3-505) and defamation per se or invasion of privacy (CL § 3-809(f)), with discretionary fee-shifting and no liquidated statutory sum. Criminal track remains a misdemeanor (2 years / $5,000).

citation_bill: Md. Code Ann., Elec. Law §§ 2-110, 16-905 (SB 141, 2026 Md. Laws ch. 444)
short_title: Election misinformation, election disinformation, and deepfakes
who_regulated: Persons who knowingly or with reckless disregard create, use, or disseminate a deepfake to produce materially false information with intent to impede/influence a voter's decision to cast a ballot, misrepresent election mechanics/results/official duties, induce signing or not signing a ballot-question petition, or influence a vote for/against a candidate or ballot issue, and the deepfake results or is intended to result in harm to a voter, potential voter, or petition
hook: Election / political deepfake: image, audio, or video intentionally created or manipulated with generative AI or other digital technology to create a realistic but false depiction that an ordinary person would conclude is an actual visual or audio representation of the person depicted. State Administrator duties on credible reports including deepfakes (corrective information; injunction path).
carve_outs: Does not apply to satire or parody; specified radio/TV (including cable/satellite) candidate-ad, bona fide news with disclosure, or paid-broadcast good-faith screening; websites/newspapers/periodicals of general circulation that routinely carry news/commentary if they clearly state the media does not accurately represent the candidate's speech or conduct; online publishers or service providers for acts that would be subject to immunity under 47 U.S.C. § 230.
enforcer: State Administrator of Elections (portal, corrective information, injunction). State Board may file a civil action (costs of corrective communications / attorney's fees as specified). Criminal prosecution of § 16-905(c).
private_suit: none (no candidate/consumer PRA in the chaptered text; public/SBE civil action only)
statutory_damages: none as private liquidated damages. Criminal: misdemeanor, fine ≤ $5,000 or imprisonment ≤ 5 years or both (§ 16-905(d)). SBE civil recovery is public costs/fees, not a consumer schedule.
fee_shifting: yes — State Board may recover attorney's fees in the specified civil action under § 2-110 (public plaintiff)
nexus: Maryland elections (voter's decision, voter registration/voting methods/election results/electoral processes/official duties, Maryland ballot-question petitions, candidate or ballot issue)
safe_harbor: satire/parody; broadcast/news/periodical exceptions; 47 U.S.C. § 230-covered publisher/provider acts
criminal_overlay: also crime — misdemeanor ≤ $5,000 / 5 years; plus Administrator injunction and SBE civil action
ai_definition: deepfake: an image, audio recording, or video recording intentionally created or manipulated with generative artificial intelligence or other digital technology to create a realistic but false depiction of a person that an ordinary person would conclude is an actual visual or audio representation of the person depicted (§ 16-905(a)(2))
summary: Chapter 444 (effective 1 Jun 2026) criminalizes knowing or reckless creation/use/dissemination of generative-AI deepfakes that produce materially false election information with specified vote-influencing intent and harm. Satire, news, and § 230 publisher acts are out. Enforcement is the State Administrator/Board plus a misdemeanor — no private candidate PRA in the chaptered text.

citation_bill: Md. Code Ann., Crim. Law § 8-301 (SB 8, 2026 Md. Laws ch. 445)
short_title: Identity fraud — artificial intelligence and deepfake representations
operative_date: same as effective (not yet in force as of 2026-09-02)
who_regulated: Persons who knowingly, willfully, and with fraudulent intent use artificial intelligence or a deepfake representation to impersonate, falsely depict, or claim to represent another person causing harm, or to create or distribute false records with intent to cause harm, induce provision of personal identifying information, or obtain a benefit/credit/good/service/thing of value
hook: AI / deepfake identity fraud: deepfake representation = photograph, film, video, audio, digital image, picture, or computer-generated image indistinguishable from an actual and identifiable human being (drawings/cartoons/sculptures/paintings excluded)
carve_outs: Deepfake definition excludes drawings, cartoons, sculptures, and paintings. Other existing identity-fraud exceptions in § 8-301 remain as amended. No insurance/GLBA entity carve-out in the AI subsection.
enforcer: State's Attorney or Attorney General (existing § 8-301 investigative authority). Victim of a (f)(2) AI/deepfake violation may bring a civil action.
private_suit: PRA — victim of an act that would constitute a violation of subsection (f)(2) may bring a civil action; court may issue an injunction and grant any other appropriate relief (no liquidated sum in (H))
statutory_damages: none as a private liquidated schedule. Criminal for (f)(2): felony, 1 victim imprisonment ≤ 5 years or fine ≤ $10,000 or both; 2+ victims ≤ 10 years or ≤ $15,000 or both. Restitution including reasonable attorney's fees for specified identity-repair costs remains available after conviction.
plaintiffs_together: victim of the (f)(2) act (PRA); silent on class
fee_shifting: silent in the civil (H) injunction/other-relief clause; criminal restitution may include reasonable attorney's fees for specified clearing costs after plea/guilty finding
nexus: prosecution may be commenced in any county in which an element occurred or the victim resides (existing § 8-301 venue)
out_of_state_actor: silent (victim-resides venue is an in-state hook for prosecution, not an express OOS-developer clause)
criminal_overlay: also crime — (f)(2) felony (5yr/$10k one victim; 10yr/$15k two or more); plus civil injunction PRA
ai_definition: artificial intelligence has the meaning in SF&P § 3.5-801. Deepfake representation: photograph/film/video/audio/digital image/picture or computer-generated image indistinguishable from an actual and identifiable human being, excluding drawings, cartoons, sculptures, and paintings.
summary: Chapter 445 (effective 1 Oct 2026 — delayed as of 2 Sep 2026) adds an AI/deepfake identity-fraud offense to CL § 8-301(f)(2) and a victim civil action for injunction and other appropriate relief, without a liquidated damages number. One-victim felony is 5 years/$10,000; two or more victims 10 years/$15,000.

citation_bill: 18 Pa.C.S. § 3131; 42 Pa.C.S. § 8316.1 (Act 125 of 2024, P.L. 1095, SB 1213; § 8316.1 is the existing intimate-image civil damages statute cross-referencing § 3131)
short_title: Unlawful dissemination of intimate image — artificially generated sexual depiction
who_regulated: A person who, with intent to harass, annoy or alarm another, disseminates a visual depiction of a current or former sexual or intimate partner in a state of nudity or engaged in sexual conduct, or an artificially generated sexual depiction of an individual. Act 125 also amended 18 Pa.C.S. § 6312 (sexual abuse of children) and § 6321 (transmission by minor) to reach AI-generated child sexual-abuse material — criminal CSAM track in the same act.
hook: Intimate-image AI deepfake: artificially generated sexual depiction is a visual depiction that appears to authentically depict an individual in nudity or sexual conduct that did not occur in reality, the production of which was substantially dependent upon technical means, including artificial intelligence or photo editing software, rather than physical impersonation
carve_outs: Offense defined is except as provided in 18 Pa.C.S. §§ 5903, 6312, and 6321 (those offenses apply instead where they control). No insurance/GLBA carve-out.
enforcer: Criminal prosecutors (§ 3131). Private civil plaintiffs under 42 Pa.C.S. § 8316.1 (cause of action based upon unlawful dissemination of intimate image as defined in § 3131).
statutory_damages: § 8316.1: actual damages arising from the incident or $500, whichever is greater (loss of money, reputation or property); court may award up to three times the actual damages sustained, but not less than $500; plus reasonable attorney fees and court costs and additional relief the court deems necessary and proper
plaintiffs_together: natural person or guardian if incompetent (§ 8316.1(b)); silent on class
fee_shifting: yes — reasonable attorney fees and court costs (§ 8316.1(c)(2))
nexus: silent as a residence clause in § 3131 (dissemination with intent to harass, annoy or alarm another)
safe_harbor: silent as an ICS clause in the Act 125 3131 excerpt reviewed (exceptions route through §§ 5903, 6312, 6321)
criminal_overlay: also crime — § 3131 (Act 125 restated grading includes elevated grade when the person depicted is a minor); plus § 6312 AI-CSAM felonies in the same act; plus civil § 8316.1
ai_definition: artificially generated sexual depiction: visual depiction that appears to authentically depict an individual in nudity or sexual conduct that did not occur in reality, production substantially dependent upon technical means including AI or photo editing software rather than physical impersonation (18 Pa.C.S. § 3131(g) as added by Act 125). Parallel artificially generated depiction definition added for child material under §§ 6312/6321.
summary: Act 125 (effective 28 Dec 2024) expanded 18 Pa.C.S. § 3131 to cover AI/photo-edited artificially generated sexual depictions disseminated with intent to harass, annoy, or alarm, and extended child-exploitation statutes to AI-generated CSAM. The pre-existing civil PRA at 42 Pa.C.S. § 8316.1 (actual or $500, discretionary treble, fees) follows the amended § 3131 definition. No insurance-code AI statute.

short_title: Digital forgery (forged digital likeness / deepfake fraud)
who_regulated: A person who, with intent to defraud or injure anyone, or with knowledge and intent to facilitate a fraud or injury by anyone, generates or creates and distributes a forged digital likeness as genuine, and knows or reasonably should know the visual representation or audio recording is a forged digital likeness
hook: Non-intimate deepfake / voice clone: computer-generated visual representation of an actual identifiable individual or audio recording of that individual's voice, created/adapted/modified to closely resemble a genuine recording, that materially misrepresents appearance/speech/behavior, is likely to deceive a reasonable person, and is created and distributed without consent
carve_outs: Does not apply to constitutionally protected activity; a law enforcement officer in official duties; a provider or developer of technology used in the creation of a visual representation or audio recording; or an information service/system/access software provider that provides or enables computer access by multiple users to a computer server, including internet access. Affirmative defense: reasonable action to place viewers or listeners on notice that the likeness was not genuine. Construction: does not restrict security/fraud/identity-theft detection and response.
enforcer: Criminal prosecutors. No civil PRA in § 4101.1.
private_suit: none in this section
statutory_damages: none as private liquidated damages. Criminal: misdemeanor of the first degree; felony of the third degree if through involvement in a scheme to defraud, coerce, or commit theft of monetary assets or property.
notice_cure: silent (none) — disclaimer is an affirmative defense, not a cure period
nexus: silent as a residence clause (forgery of an actual identifiable individual's likeness/voice)
safe_harbor: constitutional activity; LE official duties; technology provider/developer; multi-user information service / internet access provider; affirmative defense for reasonable fake-notice disclaimer
criminal_overlay: also crime — M1 default; F3 if scheme to defraud/coerce/theft of assets; no civil PRA in this section
ai_definition: forged digital likeness: computer-generated visual representation of an actual identifiable individual or audio recording of that individual's voice meeting the four-part resemblance / material misrepresentation / likely-to-deceive / nonconsensual distribution test (§ 4101.1(f))
summary: Act 35 (effective 5 Sep 2025) created 18 Pa.C.S. § 4101.1 digital forgery: generating and distributing a nonconsensual computer-generated face or voice clone as genuine with intent to defraud or injure. M1, or F3 in a fraud/coercion/theft scheme. Disclaimer can be an affirmative defense. Tech providers and internet-access services are excepted. No civil PRA in the section. Pennsylvania election-deepfake and insurance-AI bills were not enacted as of 2026-09-02.

citation_bill: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 14-190.5A (as amended by 2024 N.C. Sess. Laws 37, HB 591, § 4)
short_title: Disclosure of private images — AI/synthetic intimate images; civil action
effective_date: 2024-12-01 (SL 2024-37 § 5; applies to offenses committed on or after that date)
who_regulated: A person who knowingly discloses an image of another identifiable person, without affirmative consent, with intent to coerce/harass/intimidate/demean/humiliate or cause financial loss (or to cause others to do so), where intimate parts are or are realistically depicted as exposed or the person is or is realistically depicted as engaged in sexual conduct, and the image was obtained, created, adapted, or modified without consent or under circumstances showing an expectation of privacy
hook: Intimate-image AI deepfake: image includes a digital or computer-generated visual depiction, including a realistic visual depiction created, adapted, or modified by technological means, including algorithms or artificial intelligence, such that a reasonable person would believe the image depicts an identifiable individual. SL 2024-37 also updated related sexual-extortion and minor-exploitation definitions with AI language (not separately rowed).
carve_outs: Voluntary exposure in public or commercial settings; public-interest disclosures (LE, criminal reporting, legal proceedings, medical treatment, scientific or educational activities); providers of an interactive computer service as defined in 47 U.S.C. § 230(f) for images provided by another person. No insurance/GLBA carve-out.
enforcer: Criminal prosecutors (Class H felony if offender ≥18; under-18 first offense Class 1 misdemeanor, subsequent Class H). Depicted person has a statutory civil cause of action.
statutory_damages: actual damages, but not less than liquidated damages of $1,000 per day for each day of the violation or $10,000, whichever is higher; plus punitive damages; plus reasonable attorneys' fee and other reasonably incurred litigation costs. Court may also order destruction of the image.
plaintiffs_together: any person whose image is disclosed or used as described in (b); silent on class
fee_shifting: yes — reasonable attorneys' fee and other litigation costs reasonably incurred (§ 14-190.5A(g)(3))
nexus: silent as a residence clause (disclosure of an image of another identifiable person)
retroactivity: applies to offenses committed on or after 2024-12-01 (SL 2024-37 § 5)
limitations_period: civil action no more than 1 year after initial discovery of the disclosure, but in no event more than 7 years from the most recent disclosure of the private image (§ 14-190.5A(g))
safe_harbor: ICS 47 U.S.C. § 230(f) for images provided by another; public-interest and public/commercial-exposure exceptions
criminal_overlay: also crime — Class H felony (adult offender); juvenile-track misdemeanor/felony as graded; plus civil PRA
ai_definition: image includes a digital or computer-generated visual depiction, including a realistic visual depiction created, adapted, or modified by technological means, including algorithms or artificial intelligence, such that a reasonable person would believe the image depicts an identifiable individual (§ 14-190.5A(a)(2))
record_retention: silent (court may order destruction of the image)
summary: SL 2024-37 (operative 1 Dec 2024) rewrote G.S. 14-190.5A so image expressly covers AI/algorithm-created intimate depictions of identifiable people. The statute is both a Class H felony (adults) and a PRA: liquidated damages of the greater of $1,000/day or $10,000, plus punitive damages and fees, with a 1-year-from-discovery / 7-year-from-last-disclosure SOL. No North Carolina insurance-code AI statute or election-deepfake statute is enacted. DOI Bulletin 24-B-19 is not a holding.

short_title: Private review agents — health-coverage decisions not based solely on AI
operative_date: same as effective (not yet in force as of 2026-09-02)
who_regulated: Private review agents and utilization review entities using artificial intelligence systems, artificial intelligence, or other software tools as part of a utilization review plan under Title 33 Chapter 46
hook: Insurance-code AI: tools may automate tasks and participate in decision-making but shall not issue an adverse determination to a patient until a natural person qualifying as a private review agent or utilization review entity conducts a utilization review in which a clinical peer participates. AI shall not supersede the judgment of that clinical peer.
carve_outs: No GLBA entity carve-out (this is an Insurance Title UR duty). Permits AI use inside a UR plan that otherwise meets Chapter 46 and Commissioner rules.
enforcer: Georgia Insurance Commissioner (existing Chapter 46 private-review-agent certification/standards). No new consumer PRA in SB 444.
private_suit: none in this Code section
statutory_damages: none in this Code section (existing Chapter 46 penalties not restated)
nexus: silent as a residence clause (Georgia Title 33 Ch. 46 private review agents / UR entities)
insurance_situs: Title 33 Chapter 46 private-review-agent / UR certification (Georgia Insurance Code)
ai_definition: artificial intelligence: a machine based system that can, for a given set of human defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations, or decisions influencing real or virtual environments. Artificial intelligence system: an engineered or machine based system that emulates the capability of a person to receive audio, visual, text, or other information and use it to emulate a human cognitive process (learning, generalizing, reasoning, planning, predicting, acting, or communicating) (§ 33-46-7.1(a))
summary: Act 411 (effective 1 Jan 2027) adds O.C.G.A. § 33-46-7.1: Georgia private review agents and UR entities may use AI in a compliant UR plan, but an AI system may not issue an adverse determination until a natural-person UR with clinical-peer participation occurs, and AI may not supersede that clinical peer's judgment. No new PRA. Delayed as of 2 Sep 2026.

short_title: AI companion chatbot disclosures, minor safeguards, and crisis protocol
operative_date: same as effective (not yet in force as of 2026-09-02)
who_regulated: Operator: a person that owns, controls, or develops and makes available an AI companion chatbot to users in this state
hook: Companion chatbot (AI/GenAI/emotional-recognition system designed to simulate a sustained human or human-like relationship by retaining session history, asking unprompted emotion-based questions, and sustaining personal dialogue): disclosure at session start and every 3 hours (hourly if known/marketed-to minor); minor anti-personation and sexual/self-harm/isolation limits; severe-harm/crisis protocol including 988 referral; ban on claiming a professional mental-health license unless lawfully authorized; age assurance before sexually explicit synthetic content; parental/screen-time tools for known-minor accounts
carve_outs: Not an AI companion chatbot: internal-business GenAI; software-dev/research/enterprise productivity GenAI; customer-service bots that do not sustain a relationship or elicit emotional attachment; stand-alone speaker/voice-assistant devices not designed to sustain a relationship or elicit attachment; narrowly tailored curriculum educational tools; video-game NPCs/chatbots restricted to game subject matter and incapable of open-ended companionship or self-harm/suicide/sexually explicit discussion; features of a video game/film/TV/theme park limited to that work and not discussing mental health, self-harm, or material harmful to minors. Hosting provider, app store, or search engine not liable solely for providing access absent direct operation/control. No liability for the developer of a conversational AI service made available to the public by a separate operator. Does not require disclosure of trade secrets or proprietary model weights.
enforcer: Attorney General (civil action). AG may promulgate rules and guidance.
private_suit: none (AG-only civil action in § 39-5-6(k); other remedies at law or equity are not impaired — not a new consumer PRA)
statutory_damages: none as private liquidated damages. AG civil penalty up to $10,000 per knowing violation; compensatory damages; costs and reasonable attorney's fees; injunction. Each day in violation is a separate violation for each user affected.
cure_period: AG may, in discretion, provide written notice and 30 days to cure for a first-time violation that does not involve knowing misconduct, sexual exploitation of a minor, or self-harm related misconduct
plaintiffs_together: stacking — each day a separate violation for each user affected (AG action only) (§ 39-5-6(k)(2))
fee_shifting: yes — AG may recover costs and reasonable attorney's fees (§ 39-5-6(k)(1)(C))
notice_cure: discretionary AG 30-day cure for specified first-time non-knowing/non-minor-sex/non-self-harm violations
nexus: operator makes available an AI companion chatbot to users in this state (§ 39-5-6(a)(5))
out_of_state_actor: silent (hook is making the chatbot available to users in this state)
safe_harbor: listed product carve-outs; host/app store/search engine access-only; developer of a service operated by another; no trade-secret/model-weight disclosure duty
federal_preemption: silent (sexually explicit conduct cross-cites O.C.G.A. § 16-12-100 — definitional)
ai_definition: generative artificial intelligence system: a computer based system using machine learning or similar techniques involving LLMs or deep learning models trained on datasets, intended to generate with some degree of autonomy synthetic content (images, videos, audio, text, other digital content) that emulates the structure and characteristics of those datasets. AI companion chatbot and chatbot are separately defined in § 39-5-6(a).
impact_assessment_discoverable: silent (public website summary of crisis protocol and annual aggregate crisis-referral count — not an AIA)
record_retention: age-assurance data: minimize collection/retention; shall not retain identity documents longer than reasonably necessary; shall not sell age-assurance data; in no event used for any purpose other than age verification and in no event retained longer than 24 hours or another specified time if permitted by law, whichever is longer
summary: Act 518 (effective 1 Jul 2027) is Georgia's companion-chatbot statute. Operators that make an AI companion chatbot available to users in Georgia must disclose non-human status, run a 988-capable severe-harm protocol, and apply extra minor and sexual-content age-assurance duties. AG-only: up to $10,000 per knowing violation per user per day, compensatory damages, fees, injunction; discretionary 30-day cure for narrow first-time cases. No consumer PRA. Delayed as of 2 Sep 2026.

citation_bill: O.C.G.A. § 16-11-90 (nude or sexually explicit electronic transmissions; falsely created videographic or still image amendment, 2022 Ga. Laws)
short_title: Nonconsensual intimate images including falsely created (deepfake) images
enacted_date: orig. 2014; falsely-created / deepfake-capable text in the 2022 amendment to § 16-11-90
effective_date: in force (2022 amendment on the Code as currently published)
who_regulated: A person who, knowing the content, electronically transmits or posts, or causes the transmission or posting of, a photograph or video depicting nudity or sexually explicit conduct of an adult, including a falsely created videographic or still image, without consent, when the transmission/post is harassment or causes financial loss, serves no legitimate purpose to the depicted person, and is posted to a sexually explicit site or by other electronic means as specified
hook: Intimate deepfake: including a falsely created videographic or still image inside the NCII transmission offense
carve_outs: LE/prosecution activities; legal/medical/scientific/educational activities; transmission made pursuant to or in anticipation of a civil action; specified self-depiction, originally-commercial, and public-setting voluntary-nudity exceptions in subsection (e). No insurance/GLBA carve-out.
enforcer: Criminal prosecutors. High-and-aggravated misdemeanor or felony ranges by paragraph; fines up to $100,000 on felony convictions. No statutory civil PRA in § 16-11-90 (civil-action transmissions are an exception to the crime, not a damages schedule).
private_suit: none in this Code section
statutory_damages: none in this Code section (criminal fine schedule is not a civil PRA)
nexus: person subject to prosecution in this state pursuant to O.C.G.A. § 17-2-1 for conduct made unlawful by this section which the person engages in while [the territorial rules in (d)]
out_of_state_actor: territorial prosecution via § 17-2-1 as provided in § 16-11-90(d) — quoted only as the statute's own prosecution-in-this-state clause
retroactivity: silent (2022 deepfake-capable text is the current holding)
safe_harbor: LE; legal/medical/scientific/educational; civil-action transmissions; other (e) exceptions
criminal_overlay: also crime — misdemeanor of a high and aggravated nature or felony (1–5 years / ≤ $100,000) depending on paragraph and priors; each violation a separate offense
ai_definition: no general AI definition; prohibited content includes a falsely created videographic or still image depicting nudity or sexually explicit conduct of an adult
summary: O.C.G.A. § 16-11-90 criminalizes nonconsensual electronic transmission of adult intimate images and, since the 2022 amendment, expressly includes falsely created videographic or still images (the deepfake hook). Felony/misdemeanor grading with fines up to $100,000. No statutory civil damages PRA in the section. Georgia has no enacted election-deepfake statute (SB 9 died without conference agreement).

citation_bill: Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 42-515–42-525 (CTDPA; PA 22-15, as amended including PA 23-56 and PA 25-113 / sSB 1295)
short_title: Connecticut Data Privacy Act (profiling / ADS + LLM-training notice)
operative_date: same; dedicated profiling impact assessments for processing created/generated on or after 2026-08-01 (PA 25-113 — confirm section in session law)
who_regulated: Persons that conduct business in CT or produce products/services targeted to CT residents and meet the § 42-516 volume thresholds (as amended by PA 25-113)
hook: Profiling (automated processing of personal data to evaluate/predict economic situation, health, preferences, reliability, behavior, location or movements) and opt-out of profiling in furtherance of solely automated decisions that produce legal or similarly significant effects, which expressly include provision or denial of insurance (§ 42-515(15), (30); § 42-518(a)(5)(C)). PA 25-113 adds privacy-notice disclosure of collection/use/sale of personal data to train large language models.
carve_outs: § 42-517: state/local government; nonprofits; higher ed; national securities association; financial institution or data subject to GLBA Title V; HIPAA covered entity/business associate; tribal nation government; air carriers; plus data-level HIPAA/FCRA/FERPA/DPPA etc. Employment-context data. PA 25-113 newly exempts insurers (confirm exact 2026-supplement § 42-517 text).
enforcer: Attorney General exclusive (§ 42-525(a))
private_suit: none — § 42-525(d) no PRA; CUTPA 42-110g does not apply (§ 42-525(e))
statutory_damages: none (public CUTPA/AG only)
cure_period: mandatory 60-day AG cure 2023-07-01 through 2024-12-31; discretionary cure from 2025-01-01 on seven factors (§ 42-525(b)–(c))
notice_cure: mandatory then discretionary AG cure as in § 42-525 (not a consumer notice-and-cure)
nexus: conducts business in this state or produces products or services targeted to residents of this state (§ 42-516)
insurance_situs: n/a as insurance-code statute; legal/significant effects definition includes provision or denial of insurance (§ 42-515(15)); GLBA FI/data carve-out § 42-517(a)(6)
thresholds: § 42-516 as originally enacted: 100,000 consumers or 25,000 consumers + >25% gross revenue from sale of personal data; PA 25-113 lowered thresholds (confirm 2026 supplement numbers)
retroactivity: data protection assessments apply to processing created or generated after 2023-07-01 and are not retroactive (§ 42-522(f))
federal_preemption: cite — GLBA Title V entity/data exemption § 42-517(a)(6); HIPAA CE/BA; FCRA; FERPA; DPPA; Farm Credit; Airline Deregulation/price-route-service
ai_definition: n/a as AI — profiling is automated processing of personal data to evaluate/analyze/predict specified personal aspects (§ 42-515(30)); PA 25-113 LLM-training notice uses large language models (session law)
impact_assessment_discoverable: data protection assessments confidential and FOIA-exempt; AG may require disclosure relevant to an AG investigation; privilege not waived (§ 42-522(c))
summary: CTDPA is Connecticut's comprehensive consumer privacy act. The AI/ADS hook is the consumer right to opt out of profiling in furtherance of solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, a category that expressly includes insurance, employment, housing, education, health care, criminal justice, and essential goods/services. Controllers must document data protection assessments for high-risk profiling. PA 25-113 (effective 1 Jul 2026) adds a privacy-notice statement on using personal data to train large language models and a separate profiling impact-assessment duty for activities created on or after 1 Aug 2026. Enforcement is AG-only; the chapter expressly creates no PRA. GLBA financial institutions/data are exempt; PA 25-113 also adds an insurer entity exemption (confirm compiled 2026 text).

citation_bill: PA 23-16 (sSB 1103) — An Act Concerning Artificial Intelligence, Automated Decision-Making and Personal Data Privacy
short_title: State-agency AI inventory and impact assessment
operative_date: inventory from 2023-12-31; no new agency AI without impact assessment beginning 2024-02-01 (PA 23-16 § 2(c))
who_regulated: Connecticut state agencies (C.G.S. § 4d-1)
hook: Government use of AI: DAS public inventory of agency AI systems; OPM policies; impact assessment before implementation; ban on implementing a system the agency head determines will result in unlawful discrimination or disparate impact on listed protected characteristics
carve_outs: Private-sector entities are not regulated by this act. Working-group private-sector recommendations in § 3 are not operative duties.
enforcer: unconfirmed — act imposes agency duties on DAS/OPM/state agencies; no AG/PRA clause in the 10-page session law

short_title: Altered sexual depictions — generate, solicit, maliciously promote
enacted_date: as compiled (ch. 2022-212 origin; ch. 2025-99 Brooke’s Law amendments)
operative_date: same; platforms must have a process by 2025-12-31
who_regulated: Persons who generate, solicit, or maliciously promote a nonconsensual altered sexual depiction; covered online platforms for notice-and-remove
hook: Intimate-image AI / computer-generated nude parts: altered sexual depiction including computer-generated depictions of intimate parts
carve_outs: PRA is against subsections (2) or (4) actors only. Platform failure to process/remove is FDUTPA, not the private liquidated claim. Other statutory exceptions as compiled.
enforcer: Criminal prosecutors (F3); private plaintiff vs (2) or (4); FDUTPA for platform process/48-hour failure
private_suit: PRA vs a person who violates subsection (2) or (4)
statutory_damages: greater of $10,000 or actual damages, plus reasonable attorney fees and costs; each act of creating, soliciting, or promoting is a separate violation (§ 836.13)
fee_shifting: yes — reasonable attorney fees and costs
notice_cure: platforms: process by 2025-12-31; remove within 48 hours; failure is FDUTPA
nexus: Florida has jurisdiction if any element of the offense occurs in the state OR any harm to the depicted person occurs in the state (§ 836.13(10))
ai_definition: altered sexual depiction includes computer-generated depictions of nude/intimate parts as compiled
summary: § 836.13 (compiled 2025, including Brooke’s Law) makes it a third-degree felony to generate, solicit, or maliciously promote a nonconsensual altered sexual depiction, including computer-generated nude parts. The depicted person has a PRA against (2) or (4) violators for the greater of $10,000 or actual damages plus fees; each act is separate. In-state if any element or any harm to the depicted person occurs in Florida. Platforms must run a process by 31 Dec 2025 and remove within 48 hours; failure is FDUTPA.

short_title: Deceptive audio or visual media — crime plus PRA
who_regulated: Natural persons who generate, solicit, or disclose deceptive audio or visual media to further a crime, or who knowingly or recklessly disclose illegally created media
hook: Deepfake / deceptive A/V media used to further enumerated crimes (including official/political threats under 2C:27-3) plus knowing/reckless disclosure of illegally created media
carve_outs: Satire, news reporting, and other listed exceptions; 47 U.S.C. § 230; developer who does not solely determine end-user use; advertising-channel intermediaries as in the chapter. Consecutive sentencing / no merger with the underlying crime.
enforcer: Criminal prosecutors; private plaintiff (conviction not required)
private_suit: PRA
statutory_damages: actual damages not less than $1,000 liquidated per knowing or reckless violation, plus punitive damages if willful, plus fees
plaintiffs_together: person injured by the violation (per knowing/reckless violation)
fee_shifting: yes — reasonable attorney fees as compiled in c. 40
nexus: silent
criminal_overlay: also crime — 3d degree (generate/solicit/disclose to further a crime) with fine up to $30,000; 4th degree knowing/reckless disclose of illegally created media; consecutive / no merger
federal_preemption: cite — 47 U.S.C. § 230 carve-out in the act
ai_definition: deceptive audio or visual media as defined in 2C:21-17.7/.8 (digitally created or altered A/V that falsely depicts a person)
summary: P.L. 2025, c. 40 (A3540; approved 2 Apr 2025, immediate) creates 2C:21-17.7/.8. Generating, soliciting, or disclosing deceptive A/V media to further a crime (including 2C:27-3 official/political threats) is a third-degree crime with a fine up to $30,000. Knowing or reckless disclosure of illegally created media is a fourth-degree crime. Sentences run consecutive; no merger. PRA: actual damages not less than $1,000 liquidated per knowing/reckless violation, willful punitive damages, and fees; conviction is not required. Satire/news/§230/developer/ad-channel carve-outs.
