citation_bill: Iowa Code ch. 554J (SF 2417, 91st G.A.; Acts ch. unconfirmed in enrolled PDF)
short_title: Conversational AI services
effective_date: 2026-07-01 (Iowa default on bill history); Act applies 2027-07-01 (SF 2417 § 7)
who_regulated: Operator: a person who develops and makes a conversational AI service available to the public. Operator does not include a mobile-device application store or a search engine solely because it provides access to a conversational AI service (§ 554J.1(4))
hook: Conversational AI (primary purpose simulating human conversation via text/audio/visual). Minor disclosures and sexual-content/romance/sentience guards; persistent or 3-hour consumer disclosure if a reasonable individual would believe the service is human; suicide/self-harm crisis-referral protocol; ban on representing the service as licensed psychology/behavioral-health (chs. 154B/154D)
carve_outs: Not a conversational AI service: primarily R&D; a feature in another program whose primary purpose is not simulating conversation; narrow/discrete-topic outputs; primarily designed/marketed for commercial customer-service/goods; speaker/voice-command/virtual assistant for a widely available device; internal-business-only use (§ 554J.1(2)(b)). Developer of an AI model not liable solely because a third party used the model to create or train a conversational AI service (§ 554J.6(5))
enforcer: Attorney General; AG shall adopt ch. 17A rules (§ 554J.6(2))
private_suit: none — chapter shall not be construed to create a PRA under this chapter or any other law (§ 554J.6(4))
statutory_damages: AG path: injunction and the greater of actual damages or a civil penalty of $1,000 per violation, up to $500,000 per operator; penalties to general fund (§ 554J.6(1),(3)). Not a private liquidated PRA.
plaintiffs_together: n/a (no PRA); public penalty capped $500,000 per operator
nexus: conversational AI service accessible to the general public (§ 554J.1(2)(a)); no in-state-user clause in enrolled text
retroactivity: applies July 1, 2027 (§ 7) — not a general retroactivity clause
safe_harbor: model-developer non-liability solely for third-party use of the model (§ 554J.6(5))
criminal_overlay: civil-only (civil penalty + injunction; no crime in enrolled act)
federal_preemption: silent (sexually explicit conduct / visual depiction cross-cite 18 U.S.C. § 2256 — definitional)
ai_definition: Conversational AI service: an artificial intelligence, available by software application, web interface, or computer program, accessible to the general public, with the primary purpose of simulating human conversation and interaction through text, audio, or visual communication (§ 554J.1(2))
summary: Enrolled SF 2417 (signed 2 May 2026) creates Iowa Code chapter 554J. Operators that develop and publicly offer a conversational AI service must disclose AI use to minors and, if a reasonable person would think the bot is human, via a persistent disclaimer or every three hours; keep minor sexual/romance/sentience outputs from occurring; offer privacy tools; maintain a suicide/self-harm referral protocol; and not claim licensed psych/behavioral-health services. AG may seek an injunction and the greater of actual damages or $1,000 per violation (cap $500,000 per operator). The chapter expressly creates no PRA. It applies 1 Jul 2027.

citation_bill: Iowa Code § 514F.8(2A) (HF 2635, 91st G.A.; Acts ch. 1087 per bill history)
short_title: Utilization review — AI not sole basis for medical-necessity PA deny/delay/downgrade
status: in force (AI subsection 2026-07-01); related peer-review § 514F.8A delayed 2027-01-01
effective_date: 2026-07-01 (bill history default; no delayed applicability on § 514F.8(2A))
operative_date: same as effective for (2A); § 514F.8A peer-review denials 2027-01-01; e-PA API 2027-07-01
who_regulated: Utilization review organizations (and health carriers via ch. 514F); commissioner of insurance
hook: Insurance-code AI: a UR organization may use an AI-based algorithm or system for initial PA review, but shall not use it as the sole basis to deny, delay, or downgrade a medical-necessity prior-authorization request (§ 514F.8(2A))
carve_outs: § 514F.8A/8B/8C plan-class carve-outs (accident-only, specified disease, short-term hospital/medical, hospital indemnity, credit, dental, vision, Medigap, LTC, basic hospital/medical-surgical as defined by commissioner, disability income, liability-supplement, workers’ comp, auto med-pay) attach to those new sections, not restated in (2A) itself
enforcer: Commissioner of insurance. Remedy for noncompliance with § 514F.8 (including 2A) is chs. 505 and 507B procedures (§§ 507B.6–.8). Pattern/practice: commissioner may suspend UR authority (§ 514F.8E)
private_suit: none in HF 2635 for the AI sentence (insurance-code administrative/UTPA path)
statutory_damages: none as private liquidated damages. 507B penalties unconfirmed here.
nexus: third-party payment provider contracts/policies/plans delivered, issued for delivery, continued, or renewed in this state (stated for 514F.8A/8B/8C; (2A) itself has no extra situs sentence)
insurance_situs: yes — Iowa insurance code ch. 514F UR; in-state delivery/issue/continue/renew used for companion sections
retroactivity: (2A) effective 2026-07-01; companion PA peer-review and audit sections apply to requests/audits/plans on or after 2027-01-01
safe_harbor: AI may be used for initial review so long as it is not the sole basis of a medical-necessity deny/delay/downgrade (§ 514F.8(2A))
ai_definition: artificial intelligence-based algorithm or system (undefined further in enrolled (2A))
summary: HF 2635 (signed 13 May 2026, Acts ch. 1087) adds Iowa Code § 514F.8(2A): a utilization review organization may use an AI-based algorithm for initial prior-authorization review but may not use it as the sole basis to deny, delay, or downgrade a medical-necessity PA. The AI sentence took the Iowa default 1 Jul 2026. Peer-review/sign-off duties in new § 514F.8A apply to PA requests on or after 1 Jan 2027. Enforcement is the insurance commissioner via chapters 505 and 507B; pattern/practice can suspend UR authority. No PRA in the enrolled act.

short_title: Harassment — nonconsensual visual depiction including created/adapted/modified images
who_regulated: Persons who disseminate/publish/distribute/post a visual depiction of another person in full/partial nudity or a sex act without consent, including using the person’s face/likeness/features to create, adapt, or modify the depiction
hook: Deepfake/synthetic intimate image: 'another person' includes an identifiable individual whose image is used to create, adapt, or modify a visual depiction (HF 2240; compiled § 708.7(1)(a)(5))
carve_outs: § 708.7(6): voluntary public/commercial exposure; public-interest disclosures (unlawful-conduct reporting, law enforcement, news, legal proceedings, medical); ICS of information provided by another ICP (47 U.S.C. § 230 terms)
enforcer: Criminal prosecution. Sex-offender registration for offenders 18+ on (1)(a)(5) notwithstanding subsection 5
private_suit: none in § 708.7 for (1)(a)(5). Compiled § 708.7(7) PRA is only for (1)(a)(4) false crime-report harassment, not intimate images.
statutory_damages: none (crime). First-degree harassment (includes (1)(a)(5)) is an aggravated misdemeanor (§ 708.7(2)(b))
nexus: silent in § 708.7 (Iowa criminal jurisdiction otherwise)
limitations_period: silent in this section (criminal SOL otherwise)
criminal_overlay: also crime — aggravated misdemeanor first-degree harassment; 18+ sex-offender registration
ai_definition: n/a as AI — create/adapt/modify visual depiction using face, likeness, or other distinguishing features (no 'artificial intelligence' token in compiled § 708.7)
summary: HF 2240 (signed 19 Apr 2024; 2024 Acts ch. 1065) expands Iowa harassment so that a nonconsensual nude/sex-act visual depiction includes a created, adapted, or modified image of an identifiable person. That offense is first-degree harassment (aggravated misdemeanor); offenders 18+ must register as sex offenders. Compiled § 708.7 does not create a PRA for this subsection (the civil action in (7) is only for false crime reports). ICS transmitting another’s content is carved out.

citation_bill: Iowa Code § 728.12(3) (SF 2243, 90th G.A.)
short_title: Sexual exploitation of a minor — synthetic/created visual depiction possession
enacted_date: 2024 (signed; exact calendar day unconfirmed from enrolled PDF blank signature line)
who_regulated: Persons who knowingly purchase or possess a visual depiction of a minor engaging in a prohibited sexual act or simulation
hook: Deepfake/CSAM: 'visual depiction of a minor' includes any visual depiction created, adapted, or modified to give the appearance that an identifiable minor is engaged in a prohibited sexual act or simulation; identifiable minor includes a person who was a minor when created/adapted/modified or whose image as a minor was used, recognizable by face, likeness, or other distinguishing features. Actual identity need not be proved (§ 728.12(3)(e)–(f))
carve_outs: silent in the enrolled SF 2243 extract (other 728.12 defenses unconfirmed here)
enforcer: Criminal prosecution
private_suit: none in SF 2243
statutory_damages: none (crime). Class D felony first offense; class C felony second or subsequent, including substantially similar out-of-state priors (§ 728.12(3)(c)–(d))
plaintiffs_together: multiple depictions of the same minor prosecuted as one offense; different minors in one depiction are separate (§ 728.12(3)(b))
nexus: silent in enrolled section
out_of_state_actor: silent (prior-conviction recognition of other-jurisdiction statutes is not an OOS-actor hook)
criminal_overlay: also crime — class D / class C felony possession
ai_definition: n/a as AI — created, adapted, or modified visual depiction giving the appearance of an identifiable minor (no 'artificial intelligence' token in enrolled SF 2243)
summary: SF 2243 (effective 1 Jul 2024) amends Iowa Code § 728.12(3) so that possession of CSAM includes created, adapted, or modified visual depictions that make an identifiable minor appear to engage in a prohibited sexual act. First offense is a class D felony; subsequent is class C. The enrolled act does not add a PRA. Whether creation/dissemination subsections of § 728.12 were already broader was not re-pulled.

citation_bill: Ohio Rev. Code §§ 2917.211, 2307.66 (as amended by H.B. 96, 136th G.A., effective 2025-09-30)
short_title: Nonconsensual dissemination/creation of fabricated sexual images + civil action
who_regulated: Persons who knowingly disseminate a fabricated sexual image without consent, or who without consent create or solicit creation of a fabricated sexual image with intent to distribute in order to harass, extort, threaten, or cause listed harms
hook: Deepfake-adjacent: fabricated sexual image is a created, adapted, or modified image of a recognizable person in nudity or a sexual act (§ 2307.66(F); § 2917.211(A)(11)). Statute does not use the token 'artificial intelligence'.
carve_outs: § 2917.211(E): lawful criminal investigation; reporting unlawful conduct; news/commentary/artistic or expressive works; LEO/corrections official duties; other lawful public purpose; adult who is knowingly/willingly nude or in a sexual act in a place without a reasonable expectation of privacy; medical treatment/examination. (F) ICS, mobile, telecom, ISP, cable, DBS, video-service providers not liable solely for an image provided by another person.
enforcer: Criminal prosecution; victim civil action under § 2307.66
private_suit: PRA — victim of a § 2917.211 violation may sue the offender (§ 2917.211(I); § 2307.66(A))
statutory_damages: no liquidated floor. Injunction/TRO plus compensatory and punitive damages; presumed harm for nonconsensual private or fabricated sexual images; reasonable attorney's fees and costs (§ 2307.66(A)–(B))
fee_shifting: yes — reasonable attorney's fees and costs of bringing the civil action (§ 2307.66(A))
nexus: silent in these sections (Ohio PJ otherwise)
retroactivity: H.B. 96 amendments operative 2025-09-30 — not a general retroactivity clause
limitations_period: civil: four years after the victim discovers the private or fabricated sexual image (§ 2307.66(C))
safe_harbor: provider non-liability for another’s image (§ 2917.211(F)); listed dissemination purposes (§ 2917.211(E))
criminal_overlay: also crime — disseminate fabricated: F4 default / F3 with prior; create/solicit fabricated: F4 default / F3 with prior; also criminal forfeiture (§ 2917.211(H))
ai_definition: n/a as AI — fabricated sexual image: created, adapted, or modified image of a recognizable person in nudity or a sexual act (§ 2307.66(F))
summary: H.B. 96 (136th G.A.) amended Ohio’s nonconsensual-image statutes effective 30 Sep 2025 to cover fabricated sexual images (created/adapted/modified recognizable nudes or sex acts). Dissemination without consent is an F4 (F3 with prior); creation or solicitation with intent to distribute to harass/extort/threaten/harm is the same ladder. A victim has a civil action for injunction, compensatory and punitive damages, presumed harm, and fees, within four years of discovery. The statute never says 'artificial intelligence.' No enacted Ohio insurance-code AI UR statute (HB 579 / SB 164 pending). No election-deepfake statute enacted (SB 163 pending House as of May 2026).

citation_bill: 2025 PA 11 (HB 4047) — Protection from Intimate Deep Fakes Act (uncodified MCL cite unconfirmed)
short_title: Protection from Intimate Deep Fakes Act
who_regulated: A person who creates or disseminates a deep fake meeting the act’s elements; depicted individual (or a person representing the depicted individual) as civil plaintiff
hook: Deep fake: recording/image/technological representation of speech or conduct, not an original unmodified recording, so realistic a reasonable person would believe it depicts the person’s speech/conduct, and production substantially dependent on technical means rather than physical/verbal impersonation (sec. 2(a))
carve_outs: Civil/crime defenses: lawful criminal investigation/prosecution; reporting unlawful conduct; medical/mental-health treatment with no further dissemination; public-interest good-faith disclosure that the item is a deep fake (civil) / public-interest lawful public purpose (crime); legal proceedings. Consent is a defense only if a plain-language signed agreement describes the intimate depiction. No liability solely as transmission infrastructure: ICS (47 USC 230(f)(2)), public mobile/private radio, telecom/broadband, or a technology provider/developer not designed/marketed/deployed for nonconsensual intimate deep fakes that has prohibited explicit deep-fake content in TOS (secs. 5, 7, 8).
enforcer: Criminal prosecution (sec. 8); depicted individual (or representative) civil action (sec. 3)
private_suit: PRA — sec. 3 civil action for nonconsensual creation or dissemination
statutory_damages: no liquidated floor. Economic and noneconomic (incl. mental anguish, embarrassment, humiliation) plus profits; fees and costs; TRO/injunction; civil fine ≤ $1,000/day for violating an injunction (sec. 6)
fee_shifting: yes — actual court costs and fees and reasonable attorney fees to plaintiff (sec. 6(1)(c))
nexus: venue: county where defendant or plaintiff resides, or where the deep fake was produced, reproduced, or stored (sec. 4(2))
out_of_state_actor: silent (venue includes production/storage county and either party’s residence)
choice_of_law_forum: silent (Michigan circuit court implied by venue)
retroactivity: immediate 2025-08-26 — not a general retroactivity clause
limitations_period: cause accrues when the depicted individual discovers creation or dissemination (sec. 4(1)); no outer years count in the act
criminal_overlay: also crime — misdemeanor ≤1 year / $3,000; felony ≤3 years / $5,000 with listed aggravators (financial loss, profit intent, website for creating/disseminating, posting on a website, intent to harass/extort/threaten/harm, prior) (sec. 8)
federal_preemption: cite — ICS 47 USC 230(f)(2) in secs. 7 and 8(6)
ai_definition: n/a as 'AI' — deep fake defined by realistic technical (not impersonation) production (sec. 2(a)); no 'artificial intelligence' token in the enrolled act
summary: 2025 PA 11 (HB 4047), signed 26 Aug 2025 and immediately effective, is Michigan’s intimate-deep-fake civil and criminal statute. A depicted individual may sue for nonconsensual creation or dissemination of a technically produced realistic intimate or sexual deep fake, recovering actual (including noneconomic) damages, profits, fees, and an injunction (with $1,000/day for violating the injunction). Crime is a 1-year misdemeanor or 3-year felony with aggravators. No private liquidated floor. ICS and non-purpose-built model providers have a transmission/technology safe harbor. The act does not use the words 'artificial intelligence.'

citation_bill: Mich. Comp. Laws § 168.932f (2023 PA 265, HB 5144); AI definition MCL 169.202 (2023 PA 264)
short_title: Election — distribution of AI-produced materially deceptive media
who_regulated: A person who distributes, or agrees with another to distribute, materially deceptive media
hook: AI election deepfake: image/audio/video that falsely depicts speech or conduct, would reasonably be believed, and was produced by artificial intelligence as defined in MCL 169.202, distributed within 90 days before an election with knowledge of falsity and dual intent to harm a candidate’s reputation/prospects and to change voting behavior by deception (§ 168.932f(1), (10)(c))
carve_outs: Safe harbor if a specified manipulation disclaimer is included (video throughout; audio at beginning and end; image visible), and if edited from an existing source a citation to the original (§ 168.932f(2))
enforcer: Criminal prosecution; injunctive relief by AG, depicted individual, injured/likely-injured candidate, or any organization that represents the interests of voters likely to be deceived (§ 168.932f(4))
private_suit: PAG-like limited — permanent injunctive relief only (no preliminary injunction). Not a damages PRA. Plaintiffs: AG, depicted individual, injured candidate, or voter-interest organization. Clear-and-convincing knowledge of falsity (§ 168.932f(4), (7), (9))
statutory_damages: none as civil damages. Crime: first violation misdemeanor ≤90 days / $500; within 5 years of a prior conviction, felony ≤5 years / $1,000 (§ 168.932f(3))
cure_period: none (disclaimer is an exception, not a post-violation cure)
fee_shifting: yes — if a non-AG plaintiff is awarded permanent injunctive relief, the court may award costs and attorney fees to the plaintiff; frivolous-complaint path may award fees to the defendant (§ 168.932f(6), (8))
notice_cure: disclaimer exception in (2); not a notice-and-cure
nexus: venue: circuit court of a county where a party resides, or where the media could deceive and influence electors in an upcoming election (§ 168.932f(4))
out_of_state_actor: silent (venue includes where electors in an upcoming election could be deceived)
retroactivity: effective 2024-02-13 — not a general retroactivity clause
safe_harbor: compliant disclaimer + original-source citation when editing existing media (§ 168.932f(2))
criminal_overlay: also crime — 90-day misdemeanor / 5-year felony with prior
ai_definition: Materially deceptive media must have been produced by artificial intelligence. AI (MCL 169.202, 2023 PA 264): a machine-based system that can, for a given set of human-defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations, or decisions influencing real or virtual environments, and that uses machine and human-based inputs to perceive environments, abstract perceptions into models through automated analysis, and use model inference to formulate options for information or action.
summary: Michigan Election Law § 168.932f (2023 PA 265, effective 13 Feb 2024) makes it a crime to distribute AI-produced materially deceptive media within 90 days of an election with knowledge of falsity and intent both to harm a candidate and to deceive electors. A specified disclosure is a complete exception. The AG, a depicted person, a candidate, or a voter-interest organization may seek permanent (not preliminary) injunctive relief by clear and convincing evidence; a prevailing non-AG plaintiff may recover fees. No damages PRA. DIFS Bulletin 2024-20-INS is not a holding; no enacted insurance-code AI UR statute found.

citation_bill: Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 16-1023 (HB 2394, 2024 Ariz. Laws ch. 193)
short_title: Digital impersonation of candidate or other person
effective_date: 2024-05-21 (emergency; operative immediately as provided by law, ch. 193 § 2)
who_regulated: Publishers of digital impersonation; paid-ad actions only against the person/entity that originated, ordered, placed, or paid for the advertisement. Plaintiff: a candidate who will appear on the ballot in this state, or any citizen of this state
hook: Digital impersonation: synthetic media using deep generative methods and artificial intelligence techniques to replace or simulate likeness/voice, created to deceive, reasonably believed authentic, not commentary/parody/satire/criticism/artistic expression, and not created by or with consent of the impersonated person (§ 16-1023(Q)(1))
carve_outs: ICS not subject for publishing information provided by another ICP (§ 16-1023(C)). Definitionally excludes commentary, parody, satire, criticism, artistic expression, and consented/self-created media. Narrow construction in favor of public-concern discourse and artistic expression (§ 16-1023(N))
enforcer: Private plaintiff in superior court (county of plaintiff’s residence; presidential candidates extra Maricopa/elector-county venue)
private_suit: PRA — default remedy is declaratory relief only. Injunctive relief and damages only if sexual/prurient depiction + plaintiff was not a public/limited public figure + actual knowledge or failure to take reasonable corrective action within 21 days of actual knowledge (§ 16-1023(A), (I))
statutory_damages: no liquidated floor. Damages available only on the (I) track; amount unstated (actual). Proof: C&C for preliminary declaratory and for injunction/damages; preponderance for permanent declaratory (§ 16-1023(K))
cure_period: 21-day reasonable corrective action (remove/disable and publish a statement to the same audience) defeats the damages/injunction track if the publisher lacked actual knowledge at publication (§ 16-1023(I)(3))
fee_shifting: silent (taxable costs denied if defendant defaults and no intervenor — § 16-1023(G))
notice_cure: 21-day corrective action is an element of the damages/injunction path, not a general pre-suit notice
nexus: plaintiff is a candidate who will appear on the ballot in this state or any citizen of this state; venue in the superior court of the county where the plaintiff resides (§ 16-1023(A), (L))
choice_of_law_forum: superior court of plaintiff’s Arizona county (or Maricopa/elector county for presidential candidates) (§ 16-1023(L)); jury trial right on contested permanent/damages claims (§ 16-1023(O))
limitations_period: two years after the person knows or reasonably should know the digital impersonation was published (§ 16-1023(A))
safe_harbor: ICS for third-party content; 21-day corrective action on damages/injunction track; satire/parody/etc. definitional exclusions
federal_preemption: silent (ICS/ICP defined in-state, tracking 47 U.S.C. § 230 vocabulary)
ai_definition: Digital impersonation uses deep generative methods and artificial intelligence techniques to replace or simulate a person’s likeness or voice (§ 16-1023(Q)(1)(a))
summary: HB 2394 (ch. 193, emergency signed 21 May 2024; operative 4 Jun 2024) creates A.R.S. § 16-1023. An Arizona ballot candidate or any Arizona citizen may sue over AI/deep-generative digital impersonation. The default remedy is fast preliminary and then permanent declaratory relief. Money damages and injunctions exist only for non-public-figure sexual/prurient impersonations published with actual knowledge or after a 21-day failure to correct. Two-year discovery SOL. No liquidated floor. ICS carrying another’s content is out.

citation_bill: Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 16-1024 (SB 1359, 2024 Ariz. Laws ch. 199; originally enrolled as § 16-1023, recodified)
short_title: Election deepfakes — AI disclosure
effective_date: 2024-09-14 (Arizona 2024 general effective date; not an emergency — confirm SOS table)
operative_date: same as effective (no delayed section in ch. 199)
who_regulated: A person that acts as a creator (uses AI or other digital technology to generate synthetic media; does not include the provider of technology used in the creation) who creates and distributes a known deceptive and fraudulent deepfake of a ballot candidate within 90 days before the election
hook: Must not create and distribute a deceptive and fraudulent deepfake of a candidate on that ballot unless the synthetic media includes a clear and conspicuous disclosure that the media includes content generated by artificial intelligence (§ 16-1024(A))
carve_outs: Satire or parody; interactive computer service as defined in 47 U.S.C. § 230 (§ 16-1024(B)). Creator excludes the provider of any technology used in the creation of synthetic media (§ 16-1024(D)(1)(b))
enforcer: Civil penalty path: liable for the civil penalty prescribed by § 16-937(B) for each day of undisclosed distribution (§ 16-1024(C)). § 16-937(B) as compiled is the campaign-finance late-report scale ($10/day first 15 days, $25/day thereafter). Named public plaintiff unstated in § 16-1024 itself.
private_suit: unconfirmed — § 16-1024(C) says a person 'is liable for the civil penalty' but does not create an express consumer/candidate damages PRA
statutory_damages: public-style civil penalty imported from § 16-937(B) per day; not a private liquidated floor
cure_period: none (disclosure is an element of the prohibition, not a cure)
plaintiffs_together: stacking — each day of undisclosed distribution is a penalty unit (§ 16-1024(C))
nexus: candidate for elected office who will appear on the ballot; 90-day pre-election window (§ 16-1024(A))
safe_harbor: satire/parody; ICS 47 U.S.C. § 230; technology-provider exclusion from 'creator'
criminal_overlay: civil-only (civil penalty; enrolled title originally said violation/classification but compiled § 16-1024 is civil-penalty)
federal_preemption: cite — ICS as defined in 47 U.S.C. § 230
ai_definition: Creator uses artificial intelligence or other digital technology to generate synthetic media. Synthetic media: image, audio, or video of appearance, speech, or conduct created or intentionally manipulated with digital technology to create a realistic but false image, audio, or video. Deceptive and fraudulent deepfake: synthetic media depicting a candidate with knowledge of falsity, intent to injure reputation, and calculated to mislead a reasonable person into concluding a real individual said or did something they did not (§ 16-1024(D))
summary: SB 1359 (ch. 199, signed 29 May 2024) is compiled as A.R.S. § 16-1024 after HB 2394 took the § 16-1023 number. Within 90 days before an election, a creator may not distribute a known deceptive candidate deepfake unless it clearly discloses AI-generated content. Satire/parody and § 230 ICS are out; the technology provider is not a 'creator.' The sanction is the § 16-937(B) per-day civil penalty. No express damages PRA in the compiled section. General 2024 effective date treated as 14 Sep 2024 pending SOS confirmation.

short_title: Health-insurer medical-necessity claim and PA denials — independent medical-director review

hook: Insurance-code human review: the medical director shall individually review the denial, shall exercise independent medical judgment, and may not rely solely on recommendations from any other source. The session law does not use the token 'artificial intelligence.'
carve_outs: silent in ch. 165 (limited to medical-necessity claim denials and direct PA denials involving medical necessity)
enforcer: unconfirmed in ch. 165 (Title 20 insurance department path expected; not spelled in the two new sections)
private_suit: none in ch. 165
statutory_damages: none in ch. 165
nexus: Arizona Title 20 health care insurers (no extra situs sentence in the two new sections)
insurance_situs: yes — Arizona Insurance Code Title 20, chs. 20 and 26

summary: HB 2175 (ch. 165, signed 12 May 2025) added A.R.S. §§ 20-3103 and 20-3407, operative 1 Jul 2026. Before a health care insurer denies a provider claim on medical necessity, or issues a direct medical-necessity PA denial, the medical director must individually review the denial, exercise independent medical judgment, and must not rely solely on recommendations from any other source. The act never says 'artificial intelligence.' No PRA, no liquidated penalty, and no named enforcer in the two new sections. 2026 chatbot/government-AI bills (HB 2311, HB 2592) were vetoed.

citation_bill: Or. Rev. Stat. §§ 646A.570–646A.589 (SB 619, 2023 Or. Laws ch. 369) — Oregon Consumer Privacy Act (profiling / ADS)
short_title: Oregon Consumer Privacy Act (profiling opt-out)
operative_date: same; universal-opt-out signal and related 646A.578 amendments operative 2026-01-01 (ch. 369 § 12/15)
who_regulated: Person that conducts business in this state, or that provides products or services to residents of this state, and that during a calendar year controls or processes personal data of 100,000+ consumers (excluding payment-only) or 25,000+ consumers while deriving 25%+ of annual gross revenue from selling personal data (§ 646A.572(1))
hook: Profiling (automated processing of personal data to evaluate/analyze/predict economic circumstances, health, preferences, interests, reliability, behavior, location or movements) and consumer opt-out of profiling in furtherance of decisions that produce legal effects or effects of similar significance, which expressly include providing or denying insurance, financial/lending, housing, education, criminal justice, employment, health care, or essential goods/services (§§ 646A.570(10),(16); 646A.574(1)(d)(C)). Data protection assessments for heightened-risk processing including profiling (§ 646A.586).
carve_outs: § 646A.572(2): public bodies; HIPAA PHI; FCRA-in-accordance activity; GLBA information; Oregon Bank Act financial institutions; insurer (ORS 731.106) other than a mere self-insurance program; insurance producer, consultant, TPA licensee; insurance-fraud nonprofit; employment-context information; noncommercial journalism; etc.
enforcer: Attorney General exclusive (§ 646A.589(7) as operative 2026-01-01)
private_suit: none — OCPA and any other Oregon laws do not create a PRA to enforce an OCPA violation (§ 646A.589(7))
statutory_damages: none private. AG civil penalty not more than $7,500 per violation; injunction/equitable relief; AG fees if AG prevails; defendant fees if AG had no objectively reasonable basis (§ 646A.589(4))
cure_period: AG 30-day cure if AG determined the violation could be cured — expired; compiled text operative 2026-01-01 omits the cure subsection (ch. 369 § 11)
fee_shifting: AG action: reasonable attorney fees, expert fees, and investigation costs to AG if AG prevails; to defendant if no objectively reasonable AG basis (§ 646A.589(4)(b))
nexus: conducts business in this state or provides products or services to residents of this state (§ 646A.572(1)); consumer means a natural person who resides in this state acting other than in a commercial or employment context (§ 646A.570(7))
out_of_state_actor: provides products or services to residents of this state (§ 646A.572(1))
choice_of_law_forum: AG action in Multnomah County circuit court or a county where any part of the violation occurred (§ 646A.589(4)(a))
insurance_situs: n/a as insurance-code statute; legal-effects definition includes providing or denying insurance, but insurers/producers/consultants/TPAs are entity-exempt (§§ 646A.570(10); 646A.572(2)(n)–(q))
thresholds: 100,000 consumers or 25,000 + 25% revenue from sale of personal data
retroactivity: operative 2024-07-01; assessments/duties not stated as retroactive
limitations_period: AG shall bring an action within five years after the date of the last act of a controller that constituted the violation (§ 646A.589(5) as operative 2026-01-01)
safe_harbor: listed processing permissions § 646A.572(3); controller bears burden on exemption (§ 646A.572(7))
federal_preemption: cite — HIPAA, FCRA, GLBA, DPPA, FERPA, Airline Deregulation (price/route/service) in § 646A.572(2)
ai_definition: n/a as AI — profiling is automated processing of personal data to evaluate/analyze/predict specified personal aspects (§ 646A.570(16))
impact_assessment_discoverable: data protection assessments: AG holds them in confidence and may not disclose except to listed persons; AG may use in investigations/actions (§ 646A.589(3))
summary: Oregon’s Consumer Privacy Act (2023 ch. 369) is in force. The AI/ADS hook is the right to opt out of profiling in furtherance of decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, a category that includes insurance, employment, housing, credit, education, health care, criminal justice, and essential goods. Insurers and insurance producers/consultants/TPAs are entity-exempt, as is GLBA information and Bank Act FIs. AG-only; $7,500 per violation; express no PRA. 30-day AG cure ended 1 Jan 2026. Five-year AG limitations period.

hook: Campaign communication that includes synthetic media (image/audio/video of appearance, speech, or conduct intentionally manipulated with AI techniques or similar digital technology to create a realistic but false recording that a reasonable person would believe occurred and that produces a materially different impression than the unaltered original) must include a disclosure that the media has been manipulated
carve_outs: Measure summary states exemptions for certain entities and content (satire/parody reported in secondary writeups). Isolated exemption sentences unconfirmed from enrolled PDF (OLIS fetch empty this pass).
enforcer: Secretary of State may institute proceedings to enjoin. Attorney General may institute proceedings to enjoin a violation by the Secretary of State, a candidate for that office, or a committee/person supporting them. Circuit court; priority hearing; injunction without proof of injury.

summary: SB 1571 (2024 ch. 62, emergency) requires a disclosure whenever an Oregon campaign communication includes AI/synthetic media that realistically but falsely depicts a person’s appearance, speech, or conduct. The Secretary of State (or AG when the Secretary is implicated) may seek an injunction; the circuit court imposes a civil penalty of not more than $10,000. Enrolled PDF did not render in this pass; exemption list and fee-shifting remain partly unconfirmed. No private damages PRA in the text reviewed.

short_title: Artificial intelligence companions

who_regulated: Operators of artificial intelligence companions and artificial intelligence companion platforms (full operator definition unconfirmed — enrolled PDF fetch empty this pass)
hook: Companion chatbot: notice that the user is interacting with artificial output if a reasonable person would believe they were interacting with a natural person; suicide/self-harm detection and prevention protocol with crisis-lifeline referral and clinically informed intervention; extra minor statements/disclosures; ban on specified engagement-maximizing dark patterns (variable rewards, guilt/abandonment messages when the user tries to leave, material misrepresentation of identity/capabilities/training); annual public incident/protocol report

enacted_date: 2025 session enrolled; signed-date calendar unconfirmed on NELIS list pulled 2026-09-02

hook: Election synthetic media: communications in support/opposition of a candidate/party, issue advocacy intending to influence an election, or contribution-solicitations that include synthetic media (GAN/AI/GenAI-manipulated image/audio/video of a person) must disclose 'This (image/video/audio) has been manipulated' (video entire duration; audio beginning, end, and every 2 minutes if >2 min)

citation_bill: NRS chs. 391, 433, 629 (AB 406, 83rd Sess. 2025) — AI in schools and professional mental/behavioral health care

carve_outs: Self-help materials that do not purport to offer professional care; AI designed for licensed-provider administrative support (scheduling, records, billing, operational data, session notes) in conformity with sec. 8(2); school personnel may use AI for admin support and under the DOE policy (secs. 2(3), 7(6), 8(2))

out_of_state_actor: AI provider who makes a system available for use by a person in this State (sec. 7)
safe_harbor: admin-support and self-help exceptions quoted above
criminal_overlay: civil penalty + professional discipline; no new crime in this act
federal_preemption: cite — HIPAA/HITECH and NRS 439.581-.597 apply to admin-support use (sec. 8(3))
ai_definition: machine-based system that, for any explicit or implicit objective, infers from inputs how to generate outputs (content, decisions, predictions or recommendations) that can influence physical or virtual environments (secs. 2(4), 7(7), 8(6))
summary: AB 406 (operative 1 Jul 2025) is Nevada's enacted AI-therapy statute. Public schools may not use AI to perform counselor/psychologist/social-worker mental-health functions. AI providers may not market or program a system as professional mental/behavioral health care for users in Nevada, on pain of a Division civil penalty up to $15,000 per violation. Licensed MH/BH providers may not use AI in direct patient care but may use it for listed administrative support if they independently review certain AI-generated reports and comply with HIPAA/HITECH. No PRA.

carve_outs: silent in the definitional/prohibition amendments reviewed (existing defenses in the pornography-of-minors chapter not restated)

First-offense distribution is a category B felony; subsequent is category A. Possession is separately criminalized. No civil PRA.

citation_bill: Wis. Stat. § 11.1303(2m) (2023 Wisconsin Act 123)

citation_bill: Wis. Stat. § 948.125 (2023 Wisconsin Act 224)
short_title: Virtual representation of child sexual abuse (CG CSAM)
who_regulated: Person who possesses, produces, or distributes a virtual representation of child sexual abuse (computer-generated depiction of a purported child)
hook: AI CSAM: receive, distribute, produce, possess, or access with intent to view obscene material that contains a depiction of a purported child engaging in sexually explicit conduct, with knowledge of possession/access and knowledge or reason to know the content
carve_outs: obscenity elements (prurient / patently offensive / lacks serious value) are required; not a depiction of an actual identified child (that is § 948.12)
enforcer: criminal prosecution; Wis. Stat. § 939.617 minimum confinement may apply
private_suit: none in Act 224
statutory_damages: none
nexus: silent
criminal_overlay: Class D felony; Class I felony if the actor is under 18 when the offense occurs. § 939.617 minimum confinement may overlay — confirm as applied to 948.125
ai_definition: Depiction of a purported child: a visual representation that appears to depict an actual child but may or may not depict an actual child. Obscene material includes a digital or computer-generated image or picture that meets the three-part obscenity test (§ 948.125(1))
summary: 2023 Act 224 created Wis. Stat. § 948.125 (in force 29 Mar 2024). It is a Class D felony (Class I if the actor is under 18) to receive, distribute, produce, possess, or access with intent to view obscene computer-generated or other material that contains a depiction of a purported child engaging in sexually explicit conduct. Crime only; no civil PRA.

citation_bill: IC 24-15 (P.L.94-2023 / SEA 5) — Indiana Consumer Data Protection Act
short_title: Consumer data protection — profiling opt-out (includes insurance effects)
enacted_date: 2023 (P.L.94-2023); calendar signed day unconfirmed this pass
who_regulated: Controller that conducts business in Indiana or produces products/services targeted to Indiana residents and, in the preceding calendar year, controlled/processed personal data of at least 100,000 consumers, or of at least 25,000 consumers and derived more than 50% of gross revenue from the sale of personal data (confirm compiled IC 24-15-1-1)
hook: ADS/profiling: consumer right to opt out of profiling in furtherance of decisions that produce legal or similarly significant effects concerning the consumer; those effects include provision or denial of insurance (confirm compiled definitional section)
carve_outs: GLBA financial institutions/data and other VCDPA-style entity and data exemptions (confirm compiled IC 24-15-1-2 / 24-15-1-3). Not a biometric private-damages statute.
enforcer: Attorney General exclusive (IC 24-15-10)
private_suit: none — article does not provide a PRA (IC 24-15-10; confirm compiled no-PRA sentence)
statutory_damages: AG civil penalty up to $7,500 per violation (not a private liquidated PRA)
cure_period: permanent 30-day cure after written notice (IC 24-15-10-4 — confirm compiled)
nexus: conducts business in Indiana or products/services targeted to Indiana residents plus volume thresholds
out_of_state_actor: yes if targeted to Indiana residents and thresholds met
insurance_situs: n/a (profiling legal-effect category includes insurance; not an insurance-code UR statute)
thresholds: 100,000 consumers, or 25,000 consumers and >50% gross revenue from sale of personal data (confirm compiled)
retroactivity: article effective 2026-01-01; assessments/other delayed duties confirm compiled
ai_definition: profiling as automated processing of personal data to evaluate/predict personal aspects (confirm compiled definition)
impact_assessment_discoverable: data protection assessments to AG in an investigation (typical VCDPA; confirm compiled IC 24-15-7)
summary: ICDPA (IC 24-15; P.L.94-2023) took effect 1 Jan 2026. Consumers may opt out of profiling in furtherance of solely/automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, a category that includes insurance. AG-only enforcement; up to $7,500 per violation; permanent 30-day cure. No PRA. Not a BIPA-style biometric damages statute. Compiled exemption and profiling-definition cites should be re-read on iga before pleading.

citation_bill: IC 3-9-8 (HEA 1133, P.L.81-2024) — fabricated media in election communications

citation_bill: IC 34-21.5 and IC 35-45-4-8 (HEA 1047, P.L.79-2024) — intimate image includes AI/CG
short_title: Nonconsensual intimate image (civil + crime) — AI/computer-generated
enacted_date: 2024 (P.L.79-2024); signed-day calendar unconfirmed; enrolled PDF fetch this pass was a stub
who_regulated: Person who discloses an intimate image (including AI/CG) of an identifiable individual without consent under IC 34-21.5; person who distributes an intimate image appearing to depict the alleged victim under IC 35-45-4-8
hook: Intimate deepfake: intimate image includes a photograph, digital image, computer-generated image, or video of an individual created or modified by computer software, AI, application, or other digital means that a reasonable person would believe is an authentic image of the depicted person
carve_outs: news media and internet/cloud service providers from the crime under specified circumstances (HEA 1047 digest). Civil chapter exceptions in IC 34-21.5-2 — confirm compiled.
enforcer: depicted individual (civil); criminal prosecution for 35-45-4-8
private_suit: PRA — IC 34-21.5-3: greater of actual (economic and noneconomic, including ED) or statutory damages not to exceed $10,000 against each defendant for all known disclosures + monetary gain + punitive + reasonable attorney’s fees, costs, and injunctive relief (IC 34-21.5-3-2). Punitive not subject to IC 34-51-3 caps.
statutory_damages: not to exceed $10,000 per defendant for all disclosures known or that became known during the action (not a per-image floor)
fee_shifting: prevailing plaintiff entitled to reasonable attorney’s fees and costs (IC 34-21.5-3-2(c))
nexus: silent
criminal_overlay: IC 35-45-4-8 Class A misdemeanor; Level 6 felony with a prior under the statute
ai_definition: intimate image includes images created or modified by a computer software program, artificial intelligence, application, or other digital manipulation that a reasonable person would believe depicts the person (HEA 1047; confirm compiled 34-21.5-2-4 / 35-45-4-8)
summary: HEA 1047 (P.L.79-2024, in force 1 Jul 2024) expanded Indiana’s civil nonconsensual-pornography cause of action (IC 34-21.5) and the intimate-image crime (IC 35-45-4-8) to AI- and computer-generated images. Civil remedy is the greater of actual damages (including emotional distress) or statutory damages up to $10,000 per defendant for all known disclosures, plus gain, punitive damages, fees, and injunction. Crime is a Class A misdemeanor, Level 6 with a prior. Enrolled PDF was a stub this pass; civil dollar figures are from compiled 34-21.5-3-2.

citation_bill: IC 27-1-52 (HEA 1271, P.L.88-2026) — downcoding and AI in health-benefits claims
short_title: Insurance-code: AI not sole basis to downcode; AI disclosure on PA/downcode
effective_date: 2026-07-01 (chapter effective date in engrossed/enrolled effective clauses)
who_regulated: Insurer (as defined in the chapter) that downcodes health-benefits claims or makes adverse prior-authorization determinations; providers submitting health-benefits claims using automated tools. Medicaid / Medicaid MCO carved out (engrossed sec. 0.3 — confirm enrolled).
hook: Insurance-code AI: an insurer may not use an automated process, system, or tool, including artificial intelligence, as the sole basis to downcode a claim based on medical necessity without review of the covered individual’s medical record by an employee or contractor of the insurer. A provider may not use such a tool to submit a claim without review by a provider or other person involved in developing the claim. Insurer must disclose in an easily accessible and readable manner when AI is used to make an adverse PA determination or to downcode a claim.
carve_outs: Medicaid and Medicaid managed-care entities (engrossed sec. 0.3). Self-funded ERISA plans are not reached by state insurance code (not a statutory sentence; federal overlay).
enforcer: Department of Insurance (insurance code); $1,000/violation civil penalty appears in the engrossed bill for a different/related failure — confirm which section of enrolled IC 27-1-52
private_suit: none in the AI/downcoding sections of the engrossed chapter
statutory_damages: public penalty language in the engrossed bill (not more than $1,000 per violation in a nearby section) — confirm enrolled mapping; not a private PRA
nexus: silent
federal_preemption: silent in the chapter (ERISA self-funded plans not an express clause)
ai_definition: n/a as a defined term — 'automated process, system, or tool, including artificial intelligence'
summary: HEA 1271 (P.L.88-2026; in force 1 Jul 2026) adds IC 27-1-52. Insurers may not use AI or other automated tools as the sole basis to downcode a medical-necessity claim without human review of the medical record, and must disclose AI use on adverse prior-authorization determinations and downcoding. Providers may not AI-submit claims without human review. Medicaid/MCOs carved out in the 20 Feb 2026 engrossed text used this pass (enrolled PDF not retrieved). No PRA.

citation_bill: RSMo 573.010 (2026 H.B. 2273, et al.; SS SCS HCS HBs 2273, 1946, 1814 & 2551) — child sexual abuse material definition
short_title: CSAM definition includes CG/indistinguishable-from-minor images
enacted_date: 2026-04-07 (governor approval on the TAT omnibus — confirm chaptered letter if needed)
who_regulated: Persons subject to ch. 573 CSAM offenses (possession, promotion, etc. as elsewhere in the chapter)
hook: AI CSAM: child sexual abuse material includes a digital, computer, or computer-generated image that is, or is indistinguishable from, that of a minor engaging in sexually explicit conduct, such that an ordinary person would conclude the depiction is of an actual minor, regardless of whether a minor was actually engaged in the conduct when the visual depiction was created; also images created/adapted/modified to show an identifiable minor
carve_outs: savings: child pornography as it existed before the effective date remains subject to the relevant statutes (bill digest). Doll/mannequin/robot prong is not an AI-governance hook.
enforcer: criminal prosecution
private_suit: none in the definitional amendment (crime definitions only)
statutory_damages: none (criminal)
nexus: silent
retroactivity: pre-effective-date 'child pornography' remains prosecutable (digest); not a civil retroactivity clause
criminal_overlay: ch. 573 offenses as amended (classes unchanged by this definitional note — plead the charging statute)
ai_definition: computer-generated image indistinguishable from a minor engaging in sexually explicit conduct (RSMo 573.010 as amended 2026 H.B. 2273)
summary: 2026 H.B. 2273 (effective 28 Aug 2026) amends RSMo 573.010 so CSAM includes computer-generated images indistinguishable from a minor in sexually explicit conduct even if no minor engaged in the conduct when the image was created, plus morphs of identifiable minors. Crime definitions only; no civil PRA. Do not treat secondary reports of a Missouri AI-therapy statute as law: TAT SB 1019 / TAT HB 2372 did not enact § 407.3007.

citation_bill: 6 Del. C. ch. 12D (HB 154, 84 Del. Laws c. 197) — Delaware Personal Data Privacy Act
short_title: Consumer data privacy — profiling opt-out (includes insurance effects)
enacted_date: 2023-09-11 (84 Del. Laws c. 197; DWT date used as bill-history lead — confirm session-law approval line)
operative_date: 2025-01-01 (assessments apply to processing created/generated on or after 2025-07-01, not retroactive — § 12D-108(f)); UOOM for sale/targeted ads 2026-01-01
who_regulated: Person that conducts business in Delaware or produces products/services targeted to Delaware residents and, in the preceding calendar year, controlled/processed personal data of not less than 35,000 consumers (excluding payment-only processing) or of not less than 10,000 consumers and derived more than 20% of gross revenue from the sale of personal data (§ 12D-103(a))
hook: ADS/profiling: consumer may opt out of profiling in furtherance of solely-automated decisions that produce legal or similarly significant effects, defined to include provision or denial of insurance (§§ 12D-102(13), 12D-104(a)(6)c.). Sensitive data (including genetic/biometric) requires consent.
carve_outs: State bodies (except higher ed); GLBA financial institutions and affiliates to the extent subject to Title V, plus GLBA data; HIPAA PHI and listed research/FCRA/DPPA/FERPA/Farm Credit/airline/victim-services data; employment/contractor context data (§ 12D-103(b)-(c)). Biometric is sensitive (consent) — no BIPA-style PRA.
enforcer: Department of Justice solely (§ 12D-111). Violation is an unlawful practice under 6 Del. C. § 2513, enforced solely by DOJ.
private_suit: none — chapter shall not be construed as providing the basis for a PRA (§ 12D-111(d))
statutory_damages: UDAP/DOJ path; no private liquidated amount in ch. 12D
cure_period: mandatory 60-day cure 2025-01-01 through 2025-12-31 if DOJ determines a cure is possible; from 2026-01-01 cure is discretionary under listed factors (§ 12D-111(b)-(c))
nexus: conducts business in the State or products/services targeted to residents plus volume thresholds
out_of_state_actor: yes if targeted to Delaware residents and thresholds met
insurance_situs: n/a (profiling legal-effect category includes insurance; GLBA entity+data carve-outs; not an insurance-code UR statute)
thresholds: 35,000 consumers, or 10,000 consumers and >20% gross revenue from sale; assessments if not less than 100,000 consumers (§ 12D-108(a))
retroactivity: assessments apply to processing created or generated on or after 2025-07-01 and are not retroactive (§ 12D-108(f))
ai_definition: profiling: any form of automated processing performed on personal data to evaluate, analyze, or predict personal aspects related to economic situation, health, demographic characteristics, preferences, interests, reliability, behavior, location, or movements (§ 12D-102(25))
impact_assessment_discoverable: yes to Attorney General in an investigation; confidential / not a FOIA public record; may be used in an enforcement action; privilege not waived solely by disclosure (§ 12D-108(c))
summary: DPDPA (6 Del. C. ch. 12D) has been in force since 1 Jan 2025. Consumers may opt out of solely automated profiling with legal or similarly significant effects, including insurance decisions. DOJ-only; express no PRA. Mandatory 60-day cure expired 31 Dec 2025; cure is now discretionary. Controllers at 100,000 consumers must document assessments for profiling and other heightened-risk processing created on or after 1 Jul 2025. Biometric/genetic data are sensitive (consent), not a private liquidated biometric statute.

citation_bill: 10 Del. C. ch. 78 and 11 Del. C. § 1335(a)(9) (HB 353, 84 Del. Laws c. 479) — Amelia Kramer / deep fakes
short_title: Unauthorized disclosure of intimate images and deep fakes (civil + privacy crime)
effective_date: Delaware default after enactment (no delayed section in the chaptered act) — treat as in force from approval; compiled effective line unconfirmed
who_regulated: Person who intentionally discloses or threatens disclosure of an intimate image that was private, or of a deep fake, of an identifiable depicted individual without consent, knowing or with reckless disregard
hook: Intimate deepfake PRA + crime: deep fake means synthetic media (intimate image created or intentionally manipulated with GAN techniques or other digital technology to create a realistic but false image/audio/video) appearing to depict a real individual doing something that did not occur, or that gives a fundamentally different impression. Civil action under § 7803(c) does not require a reasonable-expectation-of-privacy element. Crime: 11 Del. C. § 1335(a)(9); when the visual depiction is a deep fake, it is not necessary to prove the depiction was created/provided under circumstances with a reasonable expectation of privacy ((a)(9)g).
carve_outs: § 7804 exceptions (child/parent, public concern, etc. — re-read before pleading). News/ICS not restated in the civil remedies block extracted.
enforcer: depicted individual (civil); criminal prosecution for § 1335
private_suit: PRA — prevailing plaintiff: greater of actual (economic/noneconomic including ED) or statutory damages not to exceed $10,000 against each defendant for all known disclosures/threats + monetary gain + punitive; court may award reasonable attorneys’ fees and injunctive relief (§ 7806)
statutory_damages: not to exceed $10,000 per defendant for all disclosures/threats known or that became known during the action
fee_shifting: court may award a prevailing plaintiff reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs (§ 7806(b))
nexus: silent
choice_of_law_forum: Delaware courts under ch. 78; no DGCL choice-of-law clause
limitations_period: § 7807 SOL as compiled applies on its face to specified 7803 paths — the 2024 act did not restate § 7807 for the new § 7803(c) deep-fake cause; treat as a hole
criminal_overlay: 11 Del. C. § 1335 violation of privacy: class A misdemeanor / class G felony as provided in that section, including deep-fake visual depictions
ai_definition: Deep fake / synthetic media: intimate image created or intentionally manipulated with GAN techniques or other digital technology to create a realistic but false image, audio, or video (10 Del. C. § 7802; parallel definition in 11 Del. C. § 1335(a)(9))
summary: HB 353 (84 Del. Laws c. 479, approved 9 Oct 2024) is Delaware’s enacted intimate-deepfake statute. Identifiable depicted individuals have a ch. 78 PRA for intentional disclosure or threatened disclosure of a deep fake without consent (greater of actual or statutory damages up to $10,000 per defendant, plus gain, punitive, and discretionary fees). The companion crime treats deep fakes as violation of privacy without a REP element. No DGCL/D&O clause. § 7807 limitations period was not amended in the chaptered act for the new (c) path.

citation_bill: 15 Del. C. § 5145 (HS 1 for HB 316, 84 Del. Laws c. 487)
short_title: Deep fakes in elections — 90-day window; Chancery injunction
effective_date: Delaware default after enactment (no delayed general effective section). § 5145(d)(2) paid-broadcast harbor expired 2025-10-09 unless extended by the General Assembly (ch. 487 § 3) — extension unconfirmed this pass.
who_regulated: Person who distributes a deep fake, or enters into a contract to distribute a deep fake, knowing or reasonably should know it is a deep fake, within 90 days before an election, with the other statutory elements
hook: Election deepfake: synthetic media that depicts a candidate or political party with intent to injure reputation or deceive a voter, appearing to show the person saying/doing something that did not occur or giving a fundamentally different impression. Undisclosed distribution within 90 days of an election is unlawful. Candidate depicted may bring an expedited action for injunctive relief and damages in the Court of Chancery; prevailing-party fees.
carve_outs: News/commentary with disclosure; satire or parody; ICS/information/telecom consistent with 47 U.S.C. § 230; security-incident response; specified broadcasting-station harbors including (d)(2) paid-broadcast good-faith/payor-representation harbor (expired 1 year after enactment unless extended)
enforcer: candidate depicted (Chancery civil); criminal prosecution for the misdemeanor
private_suit: PAG — depicted candidate: expedited Chancery injunction and damages; Court may award a prevailing party reasonable attorney’s fees and costs (§ 5145(g)). Not a class PRA.
statutory_damages: no liquidated floor in § 5145(g)
cure_period: none (disclaimer in (c) is a compliance path, not a post-violation cure)
fee_shifting: prevailing-party reasonable attorney’s fees and costs (§ 5145(g))
nexus: silent
choice_of_law_forum: Court of Chancery (expedited). No DGCL internal-affairs / choice-of-law clause in § 5145. Chancery forum is the D&O-relevant enacted hook.
thresholds: distribution within 90 days before an election
safe_harbor: clear disclosure that the media is a deep fake ((c)); satire/parody; news with acknowledgment; 230 ICS; broadcasting harbors as in force
criminal_overlay: class B misdemeanor default; class A misdemeanor if intent to cause violence or bodily harm, or within 5 years of a prior conviction under the section
federal_preemption: must be construed consistent with 47 U.S.C. § 230; no liability on an ICS for content provided by another person (§ 5145(e)(2))
ai_definition: Deep fake: synthetic media that depicts a candidate or political party with intent to injure reputation or deceive a voter, and that appears to a reasonable person to depict a real individual saying or doing something that did not actually occur, or that provides a fundamentally different understanding or impression (§ 5145(a)(2))
summary: HS 1 for HB 316 (84 Del. Laws c. 487, approved 9 Oct 2024) created 15 Del. C. § 5145. Distributing an undisclosed candidate/party deep fake within 90 days of an election is a class B misdemeanor (class A with violence intent or a prior). A depicted candidate may sue expedited in Chancery for injunction and damages, with prevailing-party fees. No DGCL choice-of-law clause. The paid-broadcast harbor in (d)(2) expired 9 Oct 2025 unless the General Assembly extended it (unconfirmed).
